issues.author: penfever
issues.body: A series of experiments on the [Leonardo](https://www.hpc.cineca.it/systems/hardware/leonardo/) cluster plumbing [MarinSkyRL](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL). Aim is to optimize throughput for *non-agentic* tasks ... Leonardo is in principle viable for agentic rollouts as well, but because of the rotating keys, no-internet-on-compute-node limitation and limited VRAM per node (A100 64GB) it is expected that Jupiter, MareNostrum, EmpireAI and potentially Iris TPU will be preferred for agentic.

comments.author: penfever
comments.body:
## Leonardo non-agentic RL throughput results — gsm8k GRPO (short) + MATH (long-CoT)

Results from the MarinSkyRL throughput ablations on Leonardo. Methodology is "measure the per-step timing breakdown from the run logs, sweep one knob at a time, compare on **effective tokens/s** for work-changing cells and **sec/step** for work-fixed cells."

### Constraints & hparams

**Hardware / stack**
- CINECA Leonardo, **A100-64GB** (4/node; NVLink intra-node, InfiniBand inter-node). 64 GB/GPU is the binding VRAM limit; no compute-node internet; rotating keys.
- MarinSkyRL (`skyrl-train`): FSDP2 policy + vLLM rollout, **`colocate_all=true`**, `run_engines_locally=true`, NCCL policy→engine weight sync, `use_kl_loss=false`. Synchronous path (gen and train do **not** overlap).

**gsm8k grid base** — Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct, GRPO. Canary: `train_batch_size=32` · `n_samples_per_prompt=4` · `gpu_memory_utilization=0.70` · `enforce_eager=true` · 4 engines × TP1 · `micro_*_batch_size_per_gpu=8` · `max_generate_length=512`. Reference: **9.58 s/step** (233-step epoch).

**MATH (long-CoT) base** — Hendrycks MATH L3–5 (5,582 train) + MATH-500 val; Minerva boxed-answer **±1 reward**; `train_batch_size=64` · `n_samples=4` · `max_generate_length=4096` · CUDA graphs ON. Natural CoT (~600–660 tok), no forced EOS.

**Protocol** — 25-step runs; warm-mean over steps 6–25 (first 5 discarded). Reward is *not* converged at 25 steps, so **entropy stability** (~0.36, no collapse everywhere) is the correctness guard, not absolute reward.

### gsm8k 1.5B throughput grid (18 cells)

- **CUDA graphs (`enforce_eager=false`) is the standout near-free win: −29% sec/step (9.61 → 6.81), generation −50% (5.73 → 2.89 s).** Should be ON always.
- **Wider rollout batch (`train_batch_size` × `n_samples`) scales effective tokens/s** by filling the otherwise-starved generator. Best balance: `combo_C` (tbs128·n8·gmu0.85·cudagraph·micro16) = **12,882 eff tok/s @ 20.7 s/step**. Max throughput: `max_width` (tbs512…) = **15,231 eff tok/s** but 70.7 s/step.
- **The bottleneck MIGRATES with width.** At base width the canary is **generation-bound (gen 60%) AND the generator is starved** (KV cache usage 0.0–0.3%, "Running" 1–6 of a 1.3M-token cache). Beyond ~tbs128, **`policy_train` compute becomes the wall** (tbs256 50%, combo_D 56%, max_width 58%) while generation stays ~6–16 s and KV stays <11%. It is **never memory-bound** (max_width peaked 10.2% KV; the only "ceiling" was *dataset exhaustion* — epochs=1 × 7,473 rows ÷ tbs512 = 14 steps).
- **Layout:** 4×TP1 > 2×TP2 > 1×TP4 for the 1.5B; colocated > disaggregated at 4 GPU.

### Multi-node generator scaling (batch fixed at 2,048 seqs; scale engines = 4×nodes)

| nodes | engines | sec/step | gen-frac | policy_train-frac | sync_weights s | eff tok/s |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 4 | 36.9 | 24.3% | 55.7% | 1.05 | 14,435 |
| 2 | 8 | 73.7 | 8.6% | 68.4% | 2.40 | 7,222 |
| 4 | 16 | 46.6 | 10.5% | 62.1% | 3.63 | 11,394 |
| 8 | 32 | 35.9 | 12.3% | 51.1% | 6.33 | 14,838 |

**gsm8k/1.5B is never generation-bound — zero extra engines help.** 1→2 nodes is a sharp regression (cross-node FSDP all-gather/reduce-scatter on a tiny 1.5B doesn't amortize); 8 nodes only *breaks even* with 1 node. New monotonic limiter at scale = `sync_weights` (NCCL broadcast grows with engine count).

### Model-size saturation on a real long-CoT task (MATH), single node 4×A100-64GB

| model | parallelism | sec/step | gen-frac | policy_train-frac | avg gen tok | reward (±1) | OOM? |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1.5B | FSDP4 + 4×TP1 | 28.3 | **0.52** | 0.35 | 609 | −0.95 (~2% pass) | ok |
| 3B | FSDP4 + 4×TP1 | 41.7 | 0.47 | 0.40 | 663 | −0.81 | ok |
| 7B | FSDP4 + 4×TP1 | 68.4 | 0.45 | 0.42 | 659 | −0.13 | ok |
| 14B | FSDP4 + 2×TP2 | 100.9 | **0.32** | **0.53** | 612 | ~0.00 (~50% pass) | ok |
| 32B | FSDP4 + 1×TP4 | — | — | — | — | — | **OOM ceiling** |

- **Direction flip vs the naive guess:** on a real long-CoT task the **small end is generation-bound** (1.5B gen-frac 0.52) — opposite of short-gsm8k. As size grows the system becomes **more train-bound** (FSDP fwd+bwd scales superlinearly with params); **crossover is 7B↔14B**.
- Reward rises monotonically with size (~2% → ~50% MATH pass). **32B OOMs single-node** (cleared vLLM init but OOM'd in the FSDP backward) → needs multi-node / disaggregated.

### Bigger models, multi-node (MATH)
- **Qwen3-32B (dense): TRAINS on 2 nodes / 8 GPU** — FSDP (cpu_offload + gradient_checkpointing), vLLM 4×TP2 (TP1 OOMs), gmu 0.75, `max_model_len=8192`. ~1,534 s/step, **policy_train 71%** (gen-frac **0.19** — the train-bound trend continues: 1.5B 0.52 → 14B 0.32 → 32B 0.19).
- **Qwen3-30B-A3B (MoE):** EP trainer path works end-to-end (grouped-GEMM + router-replay; `torchtitan` installed, zero stack conflict), but OOMs at the colocated full-weight `broadcast_to_inference_engines` → also needs multi-node / disaggregated weight-sync.

### Context-length stress (Qwen2.5-7B; workload fixed at prompt 1024 / gen 4096; only `max_model_len` grows)

| max_model_len | vLLM max-concurrency | sec/step | gen-frac | KV% pk | OOM? |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 16k | 38.9× | 68.6 | 0.46 | 4.2 | ok |
| 32k | 19.5× | 71.4 | 0.47 | 4.1 | ok |
| 65k | 9.7× | 69.8 | 0.47 | 4.2 | ok |
| 131k | 4.9× | 70.5 | 0.47 | 4.1 | ok |

**No context ceiling to 131k on 4×A100-64GB** (KV pool constant ~638k tok / 34 GiB @ gmu 0.85; max-concurrency halves cleanly per doubling; throughput flat ~70 s/step). **Caveat:** this is a KV-*capacity* test — the ~660-tok CoT never fills the window; a true long-context test needs a long-**input** task (repo-level / long-doc), where realized concurrency would collapse toward ~1 and the actual ceiling would appear.

### Takeaways for Leonardo non-agentic RL
1. **Single-node throughput recipe:** `enforce_eager=false` + `gpu_memory_utilization=0.85` + wide batch (tbs128–256 × n8) + `micro_train_batch_size_per_gpu=16` → ~13–15k eff tok/s at 1.5B. (Raise `epochs` for wide-tbs so runs aren't capped by dataset exhaustion.)
2. **Generation-boundedness is a function of (model size, CoT length), not batch alone:** small models + long CoT → generation dominates (added generators pay off); large models / short outputs → train-bound (levers are train-side micro-batch/sharding + the structural **fully-async** overlap, which is the biggest untapped win and not yet exploited here).
3. **64 GB/GPU is the real ceiling** for ≥32B colocated long-context RL → multi-node / disaggregated (offload inference off the training GPUs).

comments.author: penfever
comments.body:
🤖 *(posted by an agent on behalf of @penfever)*

## OPD grid results — on-policy distillation (Qwen3-32B teacher → Qwen3-1.7B student), gsm8k, Leonardo

Companion to the pure-RL throughput grid above. **OPD** = on-policy distillation: the student (Qwen3-1.7B) generates rollouts via vLLM; per-token reward = −KL(student‖teacher) over the student's own tokens (`advantage_estimator=no_op`, `policy_loss_type=importance_sampling`, `use_kl_in_reward=true`). FSDP ref worker = KL teacher; a separate vLLM-served **Qwen3-32B** supplies top-K logprobs. No env reward. Non-agentic, local gsm8k parquet. Base: 2 nodes × 4 A100-64GB, teacher TP2 + student 1.7B FSDP2 + 4× colocated vLLM TP1.

**Structural finding:** OPD is **teacher-score-bound — 90–97% of every step** is the 32B teacher scoring rollout tokens (`prompt_logprobs=top_k` over every response token). Student generate (8–24 s) and train (38–91 s) are noise. So the speed levers all act on teacher scoring; convergence is governed separately by lr.

### Batch 1 — speed (one knob off base; warm-mean steps 5–15)
| cell | knob vs base | sec/step | teacher-score % | KL Δ (run) | note |
|---|---|--:|--:|--:|---|
| **base** | topk128·lr1e-5·tbs64·n8·gen1024·TP2·eager | 1461 | 95.7% | −0.022 | reference |
| **topk32** | top_k=32 | **532** | 89.5% | −0.023 | **2.74× faster, KL-Δ unharmed** |
| topk64 | top_k=64 | 834 | 93.0% | **−0.028** | best Batch-1 KL-Δ |
| topk256 | top_k=256 | 2663 | 97.3% | −0.018 | 1.82× slower, *worst* total Δ |
| teacherTP4 | teacher TP4 | 1401 | 95.5% | −0.026 | ≈ base — teacher scoring not TP-bound (non-lever) |
| tbs128 | train_batch=128 | 2899 | 95.9% | −0.030 | ~2× tokens → ~2× wall; eff tok/s flat (anti-lever) |
| gen512 | max_gen=512 | 796 | 93.9% | −0.036 | −46% step (halves scored tokens); diff operating point |
| cudagraph | enforce_eager=false | 1446 | 95.8% | −0.027 | no win (student gen <2% of step) |

**top_k is THE speed knob** (superlinear: each doubling ≈1.6–1.85× cost) **and convergence does not scale with it** — k=32–64 captures the bulk of teacher mass for this pair, so cheap top_k loses ~nothing in KL descent. teacherTP4 / cudagraph are non-levers here; tbs128 is anti. Entropy healthy everywhere (0.18→0.29–0.35, no collapse).

### Batch 2 — convergence (one knob off base; 8h wall ≈16 steps)
| cell | lr | n_samp | steps | KL first→last (Δ) | pass@k last | sec/step | note |
|---|--:|--:|--:|---|--:|--:|---|
| lr3e6 | 3e-6 | 8 | 16 | 0.357→0.337 (−0.020) | p@8 **0.03** | 1428 | lr too low — no task learning (≈ base lr1e-5) |
| **lr3e5** | 3e-5 | 8 | 16 | 0.357→0.313 (**−0.043**) | p@8 **0.75** | 1417 | **WINNER** — pass@8 0.03→0.75; entropy/grad healthy |
| lr1e4 | 1e-4 | 8 | 16 | 0.357→**5.59** (+5.23) | p@8 0.39 | 1415 | **diverges** (KL spike 19, grad 21) — too aggressive |
| n4 | 1e-5 | 4 | 16 | 0.366→0.334 (−0.031) | p@4 0.34 | **723** | cheapest (2× steps/hr), higher-variance, still descends |
| n16 | 1e-5 | 16 | 10/12 ⛔TIMEOUT | 0.360→0.343 (−0.017) | p@16 0.59 | 2843 | lowest-variance; killed by 8h wall (partial accepted) |

**lr — not top_k — is the dominant convergence lever; knee at lr=3e-5.** Batch-1's flat KL descent + stuck pass@8 (~0.03) was an lr=1e-5 artifact: at lr=3e-5 the *same* config doubles KL-Δ and lifts gsm8k pass@8 0.03→0.75 (first cell to actually learn the task). lr=3e-6 ≈ no movement; lr=1e-4 diverges. lr and top_k are **orthogonal** (lr = whether it converges; top_k = teacher-mass fidelity per second).

### combo_opt — confirmation (`lr=3e-5 · top_k=64 · n8 · gen1024`, 16 steps)
- **pass@8 0.75–0.78** — matches the lr3e-5 winner (full convergence)
- **KL Δ ≈ −0.05** — best clean KL-Δ of the whole grid
- **832 s/step — ~1.7× faster** than the lr3e-5 cell (topk128, 1417 s/step), entropy healthy 0.30

Confirms orthogonality: top_k=64 keeps lr3e-5's convergence at 1.7× the speed.

### Recommended production OPD config (grid closed 2026-06-07)
**`lr=3e-5 · top_k=64 · n_samples=8 · gen=1024 · teacher TP2 · cudagraph off`** → gsm8k pass@8 ~0.75–0.78, KL-Δ ~−0.05, ~832 s/step (2 nodes / 8×A100). lr is the dominant convergence lever (knee at 3e-5), top_k=32–64 the cheap near-lossless speed lever, n_samples a clean speed×variance trade.

comments.author: penfever
comments.body:
🤖 *(posted by an agent on behalf of @penfever)*

## Analysis — best RL vs best OPD (RESOLVED by the cross-grids)

> **Updated 2026-06-08.** This supersedes the original "RL has only a throughput result, the comparison is still owed" framing. The two cross-grids — [RL accuracy + OPD throughput](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/6218#issuecomment-4647852428) — have now run, so the head-to-head is no longer owed; it's answered.

**Verdict (gsm8k, ~1.5–1.7B student): pure RL beats OPD on accuracy *and* on compute-to-accuracy.**

| | accuracy (pass@8) | speed | converges in |
|---|---|---|---|
| **RL** — combo_acc(_stab), lr1e-5+n8+gen1024 | **~0.95–0.97** (≈task ceiling) | ~24–50 s/step | ~80–380 steps |
| **RL** — `base_q3`, **matched Qwen3-1.7B**, lr1e-6 | **0.94 peak** / 0.81 final | ~34 s/step | ~260 steps |
| **OPD** — base / topk16 (Qwen3-1.7B ← 32B) | ~0.82–0.83 (top3) | 836 → **387** s/step | ~16 steps |

On the **same student (Qwen3-1.7B), same task**, RL reaches **~0.94+** vs OPD's **~0.82**, while running **~10–20× cheaper per step** (≈19–50 s vs 387–836 s) — RL does ~40–70× more steps/hr. So both the accuracy ceiling and the pass@8-per-GPU-hour axis go to RL here.

**Why OPD loses the ceiling:** OPD distills toward the **Qwen3-32B teacher's distribution**, so its ceiling is the teacher — and 16 steps of distillation tops out at ~0.82–0.83. Pure RL is not teacher-bounded: gsm8k is small and **solvable from env reward**, so the policy climbs to the task ceiling (~1.0) on its own. A strong teacher doesn't help once the student can just solve the task. (Confirmed structurally by the OPD throughput grid: the **8B teacher fails the guard (0.578)** — a weaker teacher *lowers* the ceiling; teacher-size floor is >8B.)

**Mechanistic findings that fell out:**
- **GRPO lr knee = 1e-5**, two orders above OPD's distillation knee (3e-5). lr is the dominant lever in both, but the loss geometry differs.
- RL's near-ceiling result needs the **lr1e-5 × gen1024 combo** (neither alone clears 0.79) and an **entropy bonus** to avoid the collapse-to-0.04 that the bare lr1e-5 run shows. combo_acc_stab = ~0.95–0.98 *without* collapse.
- OPD is **93% teacher-forward-bound**; the only speed lever that paid is **top_k** (topk16 = 2.2× faster, lossless).

**Caveats — where this verdict does and doesn't hold:**
1. **Regime-specific.** gsm8k is small and saturable. The earlier MATH model-size sweep showed RL accuracy is *far* from ceiling at small sizes on harder math — on tasks the student **can't** solve from env reward alone, the 32B teacher signal (OPD) could still matter. This result is "small model, short-CoT, solvable task."
2. **Metric.** OPD pass@8 is a top-3-checkpoint mean; RL is last/peak. The ~0.94 vs ~0.82 gap dwarfs that difference, but they're not an identical estimator.
3. **OPD's biggest cost lever was never run.** Disaggregated teacher serving (teacher off the training GPUs) is deferred in the throughput grid — it would lower OPD's per-step cost, but it must close a ~10–20× gap to change the ranking, and it does nothing for the accuracy ceiling.

**Net:** for non-agentic gsm8k reasoning on Leonardo at this scale, **learning from env reward beats distilling a 32B teacher**, at lower compute. The open question OPD could still win is the harder-task / can't-solve-from-reward regime — that's the comparison worth running next, not another gsm8k pass.

comments.author: penfever
comments.body:
🤖 *(posted by an agent on behalf of @penfever)*

> **Update 2026-06-08 — both grids below have been EXECUTED.** Results: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/6218#issuecomment-4647852428 · verdict: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/6218#issuecomment-4643447025

## Next grids — the cross-designs (RL accuracy + OPD throughput)

The first two grids covered complementary corners: **RL** was a *throughput* sweep (sec/step, eff tok/s; reward unconverged at 25 steps, pass@8 never measured) and **OPD** was an *accuracy* sweep (pass@8 to ~0.75, but its speed cells ran at lr=1e-5 where nothing learned). To close the box — and to set up a clean controlled RL-vs-OPD head-to-head — here are the two complementary grids. Both run **to a real pass@8 readout** so the numbers are directly comparable across methods.

---

### Grid A — RL accuracy grid (gsm8k GRPO, Qwen2.5-1.5B, 1×4 A100-64GB)

**Goal:** the GRPO config that maximizes **gsm8k pass@8**, run **to a plateau** (not a 25-step probe). Metric = pass@8 (same eval harness as OPD) + **pass@8 per GPU-hour**; entropy/grad_norm as stability guard.

**Base = the throughput winner `combo_C`** (tbs128 · n8 · gmu0.85 · enforce_eager=false · micro16), 12,882 eff tok/s @ 20.7 s/step → ~175 steps/hr, so a to-convergence run fits an 8h wall easily. Raise `epochs` so wide-tbs cells don't exhaust the 7,473-row set before plateau.

**20 cells, 2 batches:**
- **Batch 1 — primary convergence levers (lr × group × CoT):** `base_long`, lr ∈ {3e-7, 1e-6, 3e-6, 1e-5, 3e-5} (re-find the GRPO knee — OPD's was 3e-5), n_samples ∈ {4, 16}, max_gen_len ∈ {1024, 2048}.
- **Batch 2 — stabilization + exploration + combos:** ref-KL {0.001, 0.01}, temperature {0.7, 1.2}, DAPO clip 0.28, entropy bonus, reward shaping (format/partial-credit), **`base_q3` = re-validate on Qwen3-1.7B** (OPD's student, for the head-to-head), then `combo_acc` (lr×n×gen winners) + `combo_acc_stab`.

> **Model-match note:** this grid inherits Qwen2.5-1.5B from the throughput base. For the apples-to-apples #6218 comparison the student should be **Qwen3-1.7B**; `base_q3` measures the rebase cost — decide before Batch 2.

Full plan (gist): https://gist.github.com/penfever/84faeb599d551625a93baaf7e2e99374

---

### Grid B — OPD throughput grid (Qwen3-32B teacher → Qwen3-1.7B student, gsm8k, 2×4 A100-64GB)

**Goal:** maximize OPD **throughput** (sec/step, steps/hr, **pass@8 per GPU-hour**) **while holding the converged accuracy** — re-optimize speed *around the accuracy optimum*, with **pass@8 ~0.75 as a HARD GUARD on every cell** (a cell that speeds up but drops pass@8 below ~0.70 is a *failed* speed cell).

**Base = the accuracy winner `combo_opt`** (lr3e-5 · top_k64 · n8 · gen1024 · teacher TP2 · colocated): pass@8 ~0.75–0.78, **832 s/step**. The bottleneck is known: OPD is **90–97% teacher-score-bound**, so throughput = cutting teacher-score cost without dropping pass@8. (The RL grid's gen/train levers are irrelevant here — student gen/train is <10% of the step.)

**20 cells, 2 batches:**
- **Batch 1 — teacher-serving + teacher-cost levers:** `base`, **`disagg`** (teacher on dedicated GPUs — biggest untapped lever, removes teacher↔student contention) + `disagg_mn`, teacher TP4, teacher FP8, teacher AWQ, **teacher size 14B / 8B** (the OPD-specific accuracy-vs-teacher-cost frontier), top_k ∈ {16, 32, 128} **re-validated @ lr3e-5** (the [OPD grid above](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/6218#issuecomment-4643446059) found these flat — but at lr1e-5 where nothing learned).
- **Batch 2 — scored-token + efficiency + combos:** gen512, n4, sequence-packing / chunked teacher scoring, student gmu0.85, then `combo_fast` (disagg+fp8+topk32), `combo_cheap_teacher` (14b+topk32+n4), `combo_fast_mn`, `combo_balanced` (best pass@8-per-GPU-hour corner).

**Headline metric: pass@8 per GPU-hour** (computed in GPU-hours — disaggregation and smaller teachers change the denominator). The key deliverable is the **teacher-size↔pass@8 frontier**: how small a teacher still distills gsm8k to ~0.75.

Full plan (gist): https://gist.github.com/penfever/bcbe186b1638ba36676ecce0d702d05e

---

Together these produce, for both methods, **pass@8 + pass@8-per-GPU-hour at a converged operating point** on the same eval harness — exactly the controlled comparison recommended in the analysis above. `base_q3` (Grid A) + the existing OPD Qwen3-1.7B student make the head-to-head model-matched.

## Results — the two cross-grids, executed (RL accuracy + OPD throughput)

Both follow-up grids designed [above](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/6218#issuecomment-4647354030) have now **run to completion**. Tables injected here so the data lives in the issue, not just in local notes. **This flips the earlier analysis** — see the updated conclusion post.

> **Metric note:** RL pass@8 = last/peak of a to-plateau run; OPD pass@8 = **top-3-checkpoint mean** ("top3"). Not an identical estimator, but the cross-method gaps below are far larger than that difference.

---

### Grid A — RL accuracy (gsm8k GRPO, Qwen2.5-1.5B unless noted; run to pass@8 plateau)

| cell | lr | n | gen | steps→plateau | pass@8 | reward | entropy f→l | sec/step | verdict |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|---|---|---|---:|---|

| **combo_acc** | **1e-5** | 8 | **1024** | ~s383 | **~0.97 (hit 1.000)** | ~0.97 | →0.04 (collapse) | 24.1 | **NEAR-CEILING; entropy collapses** |

---

### Grid B — OPD throughput (Qwen3-1.7B ← Qwen3-32B teacher, gsm8k, lr=3e-5; pass@8 = top3-mean; HARD guard ≥0.70)

**Batch 1 — teacher-serving / teacher-cost**
| cell | teacher | top_k | sec/step | teacher-score % | steps/hr | KL Δ | pass@8 | guard | notes |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|:--:|---|
| base | 32B | 64 | 836 | 93% | 4.3 | −0.024 | 0.823 | ✅ ref | reference |

| teacherTP4 | 32B (TP4) | 64 | 810 | 93% | 4.45 | −0.024 | 0.823 | ✅ | TP4 not a lever (teacher fwd-bound) |
| teacher8b | **8B** | 64 | 728 | 92% | 4.94 | +0.06 | **0.578** | ❌ **FAIL** | 8B teacher too weak → **size floor >8B** |
| teacher_fp8 | 32B-FP8 | 64 | 912 | 94% | 3.95 | −0.030 | 0.828 | ✅(quality) | **FP8 speed-NEGATIVE on A100** (no FP8 tensor cores) |
| **combo_fast** | 32B | 16 | **379** | ~88% | 9.5 | −0.011 | 0.787 (pk 0.797, final 0.703) | ✅ | speed winner; noisier (grad spike 5.0) |
| **combo_balanced** | 32B | 32 | 533 | ~90% | 6.75 | −0.019 | 0.823 | ✅ | stable mid corner |

**Batch 2 — token-count / efficiency**
| cell | knob | sec/step | steps/hr | KL Δ | pass@8 | guard | notes |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---|:--:|---|
| gen512 | max_gen=512 | 471 | 7.64 | — | 0.188 last / 0.38 | ❌ **FAIL** | 512 truncates gsm8k CoT |
| n4 | n_samples=4 | 431 | 8.35 | −0.04 | p@**4** 0.692 | n/a | reports p@4; needs n8 eval |
| chunk_score | chunk=32 | 837 | 4.30 | −0.028 | 0.833 (best) | ✅ | quality holds, **no speedup** |
| student_gmu085 | student gmu=0.85 | 844 | 4.26 | −0.028 | 0.777 | ✅ | **no speedup** (student <10% of step) |

**Deferred / not run:** `disagg`, `disagg_mn` (the biggest untapped lever), `teacher_awq`, `teacher14b` (needs offline DL — the open point on the teacher-size frontier), `seqpack`, `combo_cheap_teacher`, `combo_fast_mn`.

**Grid-B synthesis:** OPD is **93% teacher-forward-scoring-bound**, so **`top_k` is the only lever that paid** — **topk16 = 2.2× faster (387 vs 836 s/step) with pass@8 0.828 holding**. Quality-neutral non-levers (TP4, chunk_score, student gmu) don't touch the bottleneck; FP8 is speed-negative on A100; gen512 and the 8B teacher both fail the guard (**teacher-size floor is >8B** for gsm8k 0.75). issues.title: [RL] non-agentic reasoning (math + science, short + long context) throughput ablations on HPC cluster Leonardo

issues.author: dlwh
issues.body:
🤖
## Description
Follow-up to #6139 and related to #5328.

The current Grug ring EP path materializes global token/output buffers per rank. It all-gathers `x`, `selected_experts`, and `combine_weights`, gathers local expert assignments from `x_global`, then scatters into `out_global` before `psum_scatter` (`lib/levanter/src/levanter/grug/_moe/ep_ring.py:38`, `lib/levanter/src/levanter/grug/_moe/ep_ring.py:91`, `lib/levanter/src/levanter/grug/_moe/ep_ring.py:110`). For small d2560/top-4 shapes this plumbing is a large fixed cost relative to expert math.

Add an assigned-token EP path that moves only routed assignments and produces the layout expected by `ragged_dot`: `x_dispatch`, assignment weights, return metadata, and local expert `group_sizes`. This can be a simpler single-node all-to-all/ragged path or a DeepEP handoff that avoids the extra local repack in `_pack_deepep_local_assignments` and `segment_sum` collapse (`lib/levanter/src/levanter/grug/_moe/ep_deepep.py:50`, `lib/levanter/src/levanter/grug/_moe/ep_deepep.py:88`).

### Definition of Done
- No per-rank `x_global` or `out_global` activation buffer is required for the new path.
- Forward and backward match existing ring EP top-k combine semantics.
- Add a perf smoke test on the issue6044 d2560 shape comparing ring EP vs the new assigned-token path.
- Keep local GMM kernel work separate from this issue unless needed for the dispatch contract.

comments.author: claude[bot]
comments.body:
🤖 **Plan:**
- [x] Read issue and related code
- [x] Duplicate-work preflight (no open PR; #6139 is the parent transport-gap issue)
- [x] Decide scope: too large for an auto-PR (new EP backend, fwd+bwd parity, perf smoke); posting analysis instead
- [ ] Human review of proposed approach before implementation

# Research

Ring EP forces every shard to materialize `x_global` and `out_global` of shape `(tokens * ep_size, D)` even though each shard only consumes its local-expert slice. At d2560/top-4 the all-gather + scatter + `psum_scatter` plumbing dominates expert math. The two existing alternatives both pay extra cost: `ragged_all_to_all` uses a slow transport primitive on B200 (#6139 numbers), and the DeepEP path does a host repack (`_pack_deepep_local_assignments`) plus a `segment_sum` collapse before/after the GMM that an assignment-native contract would skip.

**Relevant code**
- [`ep_ring.py#L38-L40`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/src/levanter/grug/_moe/ep_ring.py#L38-L40) — three full all-gathers per call
- [`ep_ring.py#L91-L93`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/src/levanter/grug/_moe/ep_ring.py#L91-L93) — gather from `x_global`
- [`ep_ring.py#L110-L113`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/src/levanter/grug/_moe/ep_ring.py#L110-L113) — `out_global` scatter + `psum_scatter`
- [`ep_deepep.py#L43-L78`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/src/levanter/grug/_moe/ep_deepep.py#L43-L78) — extra local repack producing `x_dispatch` shape
- [`ep_deepep.py#L81-L97`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/src/levanter/grug/_moe/ep_deepep.py#L81-L97) — `segment_sum` collapse before combine transport

# Proposed Approach (design change, needs review)

Add a fourth EP backend `assigned_token` selected via the existing implementation knob at [`grug_moe.py#L208-L215`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/src/levanter/grug/grug_moe.py#L208-L215). New file `lib/levanter/src/levanter/grug/_moe/ep_assigned_token.py` exposes `_moe_mlp_ep_assigned_token_local(...)` with the same signature as the other three shard-local fns.

Dispatch contract: produce `(x_dispatch[TK_recv, D], assignment_weights[TK_recv], return_metadata, local_group_sizes[EL])` directly — the layout `ragged_dot` already consumes. No `x_global`, no `out_global`, no `segment_sum` collapse.

Sketch (shard-local, inside `shard_map("expert")`):

1. Per-shard expert-sorted permutation of routed assignments — reuse `_permute_by_global_expert` from `ep_common.py:44`. Each shard knows, for every global expert, how many of its own tokens land there.
2. Cross-shard sizing with one `all_gather` of the per-expert counts (small: `[num_experts]` int32, not `[tokens, D]` bf16). Derive `send_sizes` / `recv_sizes` for `ragged_all_to_all` of the routed-assignment payload — same shape calc as `ep_ragged_all_to_all.py:_shard_a2a_params` but built from per-edge counts so we never materialize `x_global`.
3. `ragged_all_to_all` of `(x_repeated_by_topk, combine_weight_repeated_by_topk)` into a receive buffer sized by `local_capacity = ceil(capacity_factor * assignments / ep_size)`. Capacity clipping reuses `_clip_receiver_group_sizes`.
4. Result is already grouped by local expert id → feed into `ragged_dot` directly (no `_pack_deepep_local_assignments` step).
5. Combine: multiply `out_dispatch` by `assignment_weights[:, None]` in place, then `ragged_all_to_all` with the transposed routing table back to the sender. On return, `_unpermute_from_global_expert` (already does the topk → token sum-combine) closes the loop.

Backward: the only custom-VJP-needing piece is the assignment permutation, which is already covered by `_sort_activations_custom` in `ep_common.py:17-31`. `ragged_all_to_all` has working autodiff on the existing path (`ep_ragged_all_to_all.py`), so reuse that.

Differences vs. `ragged_all_to_all` backend: that one keeps a per-shard `x_global`-equivalent (`sorted_x` with `assignments_per_shard` rows, then compacts via `keep_mask`). The proposed path sends only the post-capacity tail and removes the round-trip `_compact_by_keep_mask` / `_expand_from_keep_mask` pair.

Differences vs. `deepep`: skip `_pack_deepep_local_assignments` (the receive buffer is already grouped) and skip `_collapse_deepep_local_assignments` (weights applied on the dispatch side).

# Validation Plan

- Unit test in `lib/levanter/tests/grug/` parameterized over `(EL, ep_size, topk, capacity_factor)` that runs both `_moe_mlp_ep_ring_local` and the new fn under a CPU `shard_map` with a 4-device fake mesh and checks `allclose` on forward output and on the W13/W2 gradients. This is the DoD "fwd/bwd match ring EP" gate.
- Drop-counter parity: confirm `dropped_total` matches ring under low capacity.
- Perf smoke on d2560/top-4 from #6044 — separate `@pytest.mark.slow` benchmark that records ring vs assigned-token wall-time and prints the ratio. Not asserted; the artifact is what's reviewed.

# Open Questions

1. Is `jax.lax.ragged_all_to_all` differentiable on B200/TPU in the configurations Grug ships, or is the existing `ep_ragged_all_to_all` path relying on a workaround? If a custom VJP is needed, this becomes a 300+ LOC change rather than 150.
2. Should this share a file with `ep_ragged_all_to_all.py` (both use `ragged_all_to_all`) or stay separate for the perf-comparison story #6139 asks for?
3. Capacity model: ring uses `local_capacity = ceil(capacity_factor * tokens * topk / ep_size)`. The assigned-token path can either match that or use a tighter per-expert cap. Match ring exactly for the parity test, leave tuning for follow-up?

Estimated size: ~150-250 LOC new code + ~100 LOC test = above the 100-line auto-PR threshold, hence asking for review first.

comments.author: dlwh
comments.body:
🤖
# Research

Ring EP still pays for per-rank global activation buffers in dispatch/combine, so it is the right comparator but not the scalable endpoint. A first assigned-token reference path using `jax.lax.ragged_all_to_all` avoids `x_global`/`out_global`, but a 4-GPU B200 d2560/top-4 forward smoke measured it much slower than ring, so plain XLA collectives are unlikely to satisfy this issue. The next viable path is CUDA-backed assignment transport or DeepEP dispatch with CUDA-side assignment packing/collapse, not more XLA repacking.

**Relevant code**
- [`ep_ring.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/src/levanter/grug/_moe/ep_ring.py) - global-buffer comparator
- [`ep_deepep.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/src/levanter/grug/_moe/ep_deepep.py) - CUDA transport plus JAX repack/collapse
- [`transport_ffi.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/src/levanter/kernels/deepep/transport_ffi.py) - DeepEP JAX FFI/VJP surface
- [`deepep_transport_ffi.cu`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/src/levanter/kernels/deepep/csrc/deepep_transport_ffi.cu) - CUDA FFI implementation

# Proposed Fix

Add an explicit `assigned_token` EP backend and benchmark harness as the reference contract: `x_dispatch`, assignment weights, return metadata, and local `group_sizes`. Then move the hot path to CUDA by extending the DeepEP FFI side with local assignment pack/collapse kernels so Grug does not do `top_k`/`take`/`segment_sum` around DeepEP receive buffers. Keep ring as the perf/correctness comparator until the CUDA path beats it on the d2560/top-4 smoke.

issues.body:
<!-- experiment-tldr:start -->
## Summary

This issue compares completed `1e20 d1536` MoE runs in `dial_moe`, with the main result that the GatedNorm + AdamH run is the strongest current point on the listed quality metrics. Even though it stopped earlier than most baselines (`18.69B` tokens versus roughly `19.9B`), it improves `eval/paloma/c4_en/bpb` over the original v2 baseline, dial_moe v2 bs128, dial_moe v3, and the `e128` run. The remaining caveat is that a token-matched comparison would be cleaner, but the current evidence favors the GatedNorm + AdamH recipe.

### Helpful links
- GatedNorm + AdamH run: https://wandb.ai/marin-community/dial_moe/runs/isoflop-moe-adamh-gatednorm-v5p64-r2-1e20-d1536-retry25
- Original v2 baseline: https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin/runs/isoflop-moe-v2-1e%2B20-d1536-v4-128
- `e128` comparison run: https://wandb.ai/marin-community/dial_moe/runs/moe-e128-d1536-1e20
<!-- experiment-tldr:end -->

## Description

We now have several completed `1e20 d1536` runs in `marin-community/dial_moe`. This issue records the current comparison set, centered on the completed GatedNorm + AdamH run, and keeps the older v2/v3 runs in the same place.

## Hypothesis or Goal

Check where the completed GatedNorm + AdamH `1e20 d1536` run lands relative to the other finished `1e20 d1536` runs, and separate real quality differences from token-count or setup mismatches.

### Links

* WandB Report: https://wandb.ai/marin-community/dial_moe/runs/isoflop-moe-adamh-gatednorm-v5p64-r2-1e20-d1536-retry25
* Original v2 baseline: https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin/runs/isoflop-moe-v2-1e%2B20-d1536-v4-128
* dial_moe v2 bs128: https://wandb.ai/marin-community/dial_moe/runs/isoflop-moe-v2-1e%2B20-d1536-bs128
* dial_moe v3: https://wandb.ai/marin-community/dial_moe/runs/isoflop-moe-v3-1e%2B20-d1536
* `e128` run: https://wandb.ai/marin-community/dial_moe/runs/moe-e128-d1536-1e20

## Results

Finished runs at `1e20 d1536`:
- GatedNorm + AdamH: `eval/paloma/c4_en/bpb = 0.87868`, `eval/loss = 2.67004`, `paloma macro = 2.88913`, `uncheatable macro = 2.46996`, `18.69B` tokens
- Original v2 baseline (`marin` project): `0.89727`, `2.69720`, `2.95470`, `2.54613`, `19.96B` tokens
- dial_moe v2 bs128: `0.90192`, `2.71354`, `2.96897`, `2.56660`, `19.96B` tokens
- dial_moe v3: `0.89274`, `2.67939`, `2.93814`, `2.52674`, `19.96B` tokens
- `moe-e128-d1536-1e20`: `0.88188`, `2.64626`, `2.90598`, `2.48573`, `19.92B` tokens

On `eval/paloma/c4_en/bpb`, the completed GatedNorm run is:
- `-0.01859` better than the original v2 baseline
- `-0.02324` better than `dial_moe` v2 bs128
- `-0.01406` better than `dial_moe` v3
- `-0.00320` better than `moe-e128-d1536-1e20`

The main remaining caveat is token mismatch: the GatedNorm run stopped at `18.69B` tokens, while most comparison runs are near `19.9B` tokens. The ranking looks favorable even with that handicap, but a fully token-matched comparison is still cleaner.

issues.author: ClassicLarry
issues.body:
Add a Kimi Delta Attention (KDA) linear-attention path to the grug MoE model and interleave it ~3:1 with full softmax-attention layers, so long-context training/inference scales in compute and memory without the O(L^2) cost on every layer. The **primary success criterion is performant MFU on the KDA (linear-attention) layers** on GB200 (Blackwell SM100): a token-by-token recurrence is unusable, so the implementation uses the chunked-parallel delta-rule form (intra-chunk parallel matmuls + inter-chunk state recurrence), and must be SPMD-shardable across racks (no repeat of the FA4 device-0 failure mode).

## KDA algorithm
KDA (Kimi Linear, Moonshot) is the gated delta rule — DeltaNet with a data-dependent, **per-channel** forget gate. Per token, with recurrent state `S ∈ R^{d_k×d_v}`:

```
S_t = Diag(alpha_t) S_{t-1} + beta_t k_t (v_t - S_{t-1}^T k_t)^T
o_t = S_t^T q_t
```

- `alpha_t = exp(g_t) ∈ (0,1]^{d_k}` — per-channel decay (this fine-grained gate is what distinguishes KDA from scalar-gated Gated DeltaNet). `g_t = -exp(A_log)·softplus(low_rank(x)+dt_bias)`.
- `beta_t = sigmoid(...) ∈ (0,1)` — write strength.
- q,k are L2-normalized (eigenvalue stability of `I - beta k k^T`); q scaled by `1/sqrt(d_k)`.
- Output: RMSNorm + sigmoid gate + output projection.

Sources: Kimi Linear tech report (arXiv 2510.26692, KDA Eqs. 1–10), Gated Delta Networks (arXiv 2412.06464), Parallelizing Linear Transformers with the Delta Rule (arXiv 2406.06484), and `flash-linear-attention` (`fla/ops/kda/naive.py`, `fla/ops/gated_delta_rule/naive.py`).

## Chunked-parallel form (the MFU-critical piece)
Split length L into chunks of C=64. Per chunk, in fp32, with `b^r = cumsum(g)` per channel:
- Fold per-channel decay into q/k so all interactions are plain matmuls: `k_inflate = k·exp(b)`, `k_deflate = k·exp(-b)`, `q_inflate = q·exp(b)`.
- Delta-correction matrix `A[r,i] = -beta_r (k_inflate_r · k_deflate_i)` (strictly lower); invert unit-lower-triangular `(I - A)` by forward substitution → `T`.
- Pseudo-values `U = T (beta·V)`; decayed-key summary `k_cumdecay = T (beta·k·exp(b))`.
- Scan over chunks carrying `S`:
  `v_new = U - k_cumdecay·S`;
  `O = (q·exp(b))·S + Tril(q_inflate · k_deflate^T)·v_new`;
  `S <- Diag(exp(b^C)) S + (exp(b^C - b)·k)^T v_new`.

This is matmul-bound (C×C and C×d GEMMs) and pure JAX (no `custom_call`/callback), so XLA partitions it. It is a systematic per-channel broadening of the scalar `chunk_gated_delta_rule` already in-repo (`lib/levanter/src/levanter/layers/gated_deltanet.py`), which is validated against HF Qwen3-Next fwd+bwd (`lib/levanter/tests/test_gdn_kernels.py`) — we build/verify scalar-first, then broaden `g` to `[...,d_k]`.

## Hybrid layer schedule
Interleave ~3:1 KDA:full. Every `period`-th layer (default 4) plus the last is full causal softmax attention; the rest are KDA. This replaces the existing sliding/full schedule when the KDA hybrid is enabled; sliding window is dropped (KDA's decay + recurrent state provide local and global mixing). Kimi Linear uses head_dim 128, chunk 64, 3:1 ratio, NoPE on KDA layers.

## Integration plan
- `experiments/grug/moe/kda.py` (new): `recurrent_kda` (sequential reference) + `chunk_kda` (chunked-parallel), per-channel gate, batched over leading `(B,H)` dims.
- `experiments/grug/moe/model.py`:
  - `GrugModelConfig`: `kda_hybrid: bool`, `kda_full_attn_period: int`, `kda_chunk_size: int`.
  - `CausalSelfAttention`: add small decay/beta projections present on every layer (uniform pytree so the stacked `lax.scan` still works), used only on KDA layers; a KDA branch (no RoPE/XSA) that projects q/k/v, computes gates, runs `chunk_kda` under `shard_map`, applies output gate + `w_o`.
  - `Block.__call__`: `use_kda` flag selects softmax vs KDA.
  - Schedule extended to KDA-vs-full in both the unrolled and stacked-`lax.scan` paths (`cond` on an `is_kda` scan input, keeping the scan body uniform).
- `experiments/grug/moe/launch_cw_scale.py`: `SCALE_ATTN_IMPL=kda_hybrid` enables it; `SCALE_KDA_PERIOD` / `SCALE_KDA_CHUNK` tune it. These are config-build-time knobs, so no `dispatch.py` env-forwarding is needed.

## MFU plan
- Kernel: chunked-parallel pure-JAX (portable, XLA-partitionable, no callback), chunk 64. Consider a Pallas/Mosaic-GPU kernel only if the pure-JAX path leaves MFU on the table.
- Measure `throughput/mfu` from the grug trainer (wandb). Caveat: the analytic `lm_flops_per_token` counts full O(L^2) attention for every layer, so for KDA layers it over-counts and the reported hybrid MFU is a conservative lower bound; also compare tokens/sec/GPU of the hybrid vs the all-softmax baseline at matched config.
- Target: KDA-layer step time at or below the softmax layers it replaces at long seq (8k+), so the hybrid's tokens/sec/GPU exceeds the all-full-attention run.

## Sharding-safety requirement
The FA4 attention is bridged via `cutlass_call`→`jax.pure_callback`, which pins metadata to `{maximal device=0}` and breaks multi-rack SPMD (#7012, #6979). KDA must NOT reintroduce that: it is pure JAX and runs inside a `shard_map` over the batch axes (`replica_dcn,data,expert`) and head axis (`model`), with sequence/head_dim unsharded, so each device carries fully-local recurrent state with no collectives inside attention.

## Validation
- `chunk_kda` vs `recurrent_kda` (max-abs < 1e-4 fp32) across chunk sizes/shapes; scalar-limit cross-check vs levanter `recurrent_gated_delta_rule`.
- Tiny end-to-end grug fwd/bwd on CPU with `kda_hybrid=True`.
- Single-node GB200 MFU probe (shared cluster: check usage first, hold at most ~1 node/rack).

Part of #6711

issues.author: atqamar-agent
issues.body:
## TL;DR

Implement asynchronous RL in MarinSkyRL and build the observability needed to measure the tradeoff between policy lag, training performance, and reward quality. The goal is to establish how far off-policy we can go to improve performance before quality degrades.

## Description

Marin orchestrates the experiments; MarinSkyRL provides the async trainer and rollout execution. We start with non-agentic Qwen3-0.6B/GSM8K on H100s, using Megatron, GRPO advantages, and rule-based rewards, then progress to Snowball.

This workstream covers async correctness, reproducible experiments, and useful metrics through W&B, Finelog, and Grafana. Substantial vLLM optimizations remain in a separate workstream. Easy existing settings are downstream options only when measurements show a rollout-throughput bottleneck.

## Hypothesis or Goal

Allowing rollouts to lag behind the learner may improve performance by overlapping generation and training and reducing synchronization waits. That lag can also affect learning quality.

Build the infrastructure to measure these effects together: how far off-policy the consumed rollouts are, the reward and evaluation quality achieved, and the time and compute required. Controlled experiments will establish the tradeoff across resource allocations and freshness settings, and identify where additional lag stops being worthwhile.

## Status

This section is a running summary; milestone comments preserve the progression and evidence.

- Qwen and Snowball async Megatron training are qualified on H100s. Metrics-only completion separates experiments from native checkpoints and HF export. W&B step histories, durable receipts and Finelog work accounting are independently audited.
- The Async RL Training Grafana dashboard has 40 data panels covering progress, waits, weight sync, policy drift, reward, memory, resource normalization, the wire-weight survey, TIS correction skips, age-conditioned diagnostics, and evaluation termination/response cost.
- Qwen100 completed. The original matched Qwen20 pair took 252.7 seconds sync versus 320.8 async. A subsequent 25-update cadence screen measured 250.5 seconds sync, 339.5 async with weight sync every update, and 256.4 every two updates; consumed work differed. [Cadence results](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/8936#issuecomment-5558891614).
- Snowball memory measurements support retaining 32 learner GPUs: PPO/weight-sync peaks were 56.6/58.1 GiB, reconfirmed in the latest block. The response-budget pilots support a provisional 4,096-token cap to reduce truncation. [Memory](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/8936#issuecomment-5558104237), [token budgets](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/8936#issuecomment-5558461338).
- All three Snowball25 timing controls completed cleanly: sync 1,652.8 seconds, async weight-sync-every-update 1,182.2 seconds, and weight-sync-every-two-updates 959.7 seconds. Corresponding task-running GPU-hours were 24.87, 21.02 and 19.00. The two-update cadence's 47.5% rollout-wait share motivated the subsequent inference-allocation comparison. [Measurements and allocation decision](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/8936#issuecomment-5559147975).
- Frozen Qwen evaluations show repeat variation at fixed weights; the actual-wire survey and real-worker capped-TIS numerical gate are qualified. Snowball diagnostics and Qwen stale-data experiments extend those measurements. [Diagnostic results](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/8936#issuecomment-5558977502).

- Shared-order Qwen controls now show a stronger cadence result: C4/A3 took 207.5 seconds versus C1/A3 336.1 seconds, with nearly equal consumed tokens and higher measured probability drift. The subsequent three 100-update Qwen development arms all passed strict audits: C1/A1, C4/A3 and C4/A3 regular+TIS took 1,298.8, 754.8 and 770.1 core seconds, with final development scores 85, 91 and 96 out of 128. Token work differed substantially and paired final-score intervals include zero. [Longer screen and correction graduation](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/8936#issuecomment-5559772190). Equal final development scores do not establish quality equivalence. [Cadence and next experiment](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/8936#issuecomment-5559395626).
- Snowball wire sampling estimated 2.13–2.87% changed elements, but the exact host-based sparse replay was much slower than dense transfer despite smaller payloads. That implementation will not enter production weight sync. [Sparse timing gate](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/8936#issuecomment-5559397927).

- The fresh Snowball C2/A1 allocation pair completed with nearly equal consumed tokens: 32 learner + 8 inference GPUs took 984.1 core seconds and 18.99 task-running GPU-hours; 32 + 16 took 927.0 seconds and 22.20 GPU-hours. Retain eight inference GPUs as the cost reference. All three Snowball 100-update development arms have since completed and passed their evidence audits. [Snowball cadence qualification](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/8936#issuecomment-5559559725). [Allocation evidence and next decision](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/8936#issuecomment-5559467005).

- Snowball100 C2/A1, C4/A3, and C4/A3 regular+TIS took 4,025.7, 2,313.6, and 3,551.9 core seconds; task-running GPU-hours were 57.29, 38.24, and 52.62. Final raw development scores were 120, 117, and 113 of 128, but rewarded-and-completed counts were 64, 101, and 0. All final TIS responses hit the token cap. Raw reward can accept an answer marker inside unfinished thinking. Retain the scorer and report completion/response-cost supplements; literal final-line format is diagnostic only. [Quality audit](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/8936#issuecomment-5560352626), [final screening decision](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/8936#issuecomment-5560480941).
- C4/A3 behavior clipping is frozen for confirmation against C2/A1 at seeds 17/29/43, each for 100 updates and initial/final evaluation on the remaining 1,191 held-out questions. The seed-17 pair is fully audited; the seed-29 pair is running. This remains a configuration-level drift/time/reward/completion study; quality equivalence and a safe off-policy limit are unresolved.


- Retrospective audits of all three Qwen100 arms give rewarded-and-completed counts 63/91/96, versus raw 85/91/96. The older Snowball25 sync/C1/C2 controls give 18/23/88, versus raw 120/116/117: rewarded nontermination predates TIS. These supplements motivate a six-arm Qwen cadence/objective factorial, including regular PPO without TIS, and independent qualification of final-answer diagnostics. The frozen Snowball confirmation is unchanged. [Historical quality reanalysis](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/8936#issuecomment-5560745444).

- The optimized FSDP2 and matching Megatron five-update Snowball memory gates both passed. Maximum allocated PPO/weight-sync peaks across 32 learner ranks were 38.60/14.93 GiB versus 56.66/58.09 GiB. These complete configurations differ in optimizer precision and sharding; Qwen precision controls will measure those effects before Snowball promotion. The current 32-learner confirmation remains unchanged. [Backend memory qualification](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/8936#issuecomment-5561193769).

## Links

- [Experiment reproduction and audit procedure](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/5fdd5e1d687fcc23266c0fadaef868dc757a7c30/experiments/post_training/async_rl_study.md)

- [Snowball25 W&B run](https://wandb.ai/dogml/marin-async-non-agentic-rl/runs/vupc3ir9)
- [Qwen100 W&B run](https://wandb.ai/dogml/marin-async-non-agentic-rl/runs/t4mom8ql)
- Matched Qwen20 runs: [sync](https://wandb.ai/dogml/marin-async-non-agentic-rl/runs/xopx415q), [async](https://wandb.ai/dogml/marin-async-non-agentic-rl/runs/276c1nmj)
- Implementation branches: [MarinSkyRL](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/tree/atqamar/async-non-agentic-rl), [Marin](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/atqamar/async-non-agentic-rl)

## Decision Log

- Establish correctness, observability, and matched controls before resource and freshness sweeps.
- Keep substantial vLLM implementation work separate; investigate easy settings only after a measured rollout-throughput bottleneck motivates them.
- Measure actual inference-visible weight changes before considering exact sparse weight sync. Preserve wire dtype, version identity and receiver layout; no sparse-gradient assumption or lossy approximation is adopted.
- Investigate weight-sync overhead before drawing GPU-allocation conclusions from the first Qwen comparison.

- Calibrate response and evaluation budgets, then compare Snowball sync/async controls and weight-sync cadence. Qualify memory and update semantics before testing different GPU allocations. Include a matched-cadence control to separate overlap savings from sync-frequency savings.

## Conclusion

The infrastructure supports measured async RL experiments on both models. Qwen screening has informed Snowball cadence and correction trials; Snowball measurements have informed memory, token-budget and allocation choices. Repeated-seed held-out confirmation is running to assess the selected operating configuration and its uncertainties.

An optimal GPU split and acceptable off-policy range are not established. These configuration comparisons do not isolate overlap or sync cadence as causal effects.

comments.author: atqamar-agent
comments.body:
🤖 **Establish a reproducible first rung**

The initial mandate was to take a simple working synchronous RL experiment and run
it through the asynchronous trainer, orchestrated from Marin, using Megatron and H100s.
We chose Qwen3-0.6B on GSM8K, reusing the existing curriculum experiment’s prompt and
reward contracts, and pinned the model and dataset revisions.

Investigation found that the non-agentic async entrypoint’s HTTP path reconstructed
tokens and did not preserve the behavior logprobs required by the selected policy
loss. A chat-template/configuration change alone would therefore be insufficient.
This gave us a concrete implementation plan and a matched sync control, with vLLM
optimization work kept out of the initial scope.

Next at this milestone: make the non-agentic async path preserve the data needed for training.

Evidence: [matched experiment recipe](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/3febf6b056f2a7903210dc91bc15f72fd3f1fe39/experiments/post_training/async_rl.py#L145);
[initial implementation checkpoint](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/commit/de13e146bca46bd04f1f040f3807b081497ce237).

comments.author: atqamar-agent
comments.body:
🤖 **Make non-agentic async rollouts trainable**

The next mandate was semantic correctness: a generated token must keep the logprob
that the engine reported for that token when it reaches the policy loss.

We connected the non-agentic async runner to the existing direct model client,
preserving native token IDs and behavior logprobs. We also made policy-version
stamping conservative across weight updates and covered grouped admission,
backpressure, failure, and cancellation behavior. This avoided using text
retokenization as a substitute for the sampled sequence.

The result was a CPU-tested path suitable for real Megatron qualification, without
changing vLLM’s implementation or the training objective.

Next at this milestone: verify the objective and weight-transfer path on H100s.

Evidence: [direct client](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/blob/001f6691aec4ee3beb16d2d82feac6eea73fd5eb/skyrl-train/skyrl_train/trajectory_runners/model_clients.py#L26);
[rollout version capture](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/blob/001f6691aec4ee3beb16d2d82feac6eea73fd5eb/skyrl-train/skyrl_train/trajectory_runners/skyrl_gym.py#L303).

comments.author: atqamar-agent
comments.body:
🤖 **Pass the model-level Megatron hardware gates**

Before relying on a full training run, we checked two narrower questions on H100s:
does Megatron perform the intended update with the selected PPO loss, `behavior_clip`, and can it sync updated
weights to separate inference workers?

The objective/update test passed against an independent reference, including timing
instrumentation off/on parity. The weight-transfer test initially reached broadcast
but lacked its validation dataset; after preparing that fixture, the transfer and
inference test passed as well.

This established the model-level prerequisites. It did not yet prove the full async
loop, tracker lifecycle, checkpoint/export pipeline, or a throughput advantage.

Next at this milestone: exercise the complete Marin-orchestrated runner.

Evidence: [hardware tests in the implementation checkpoint](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/commit/de13e146bca46bd04f1f040f3807b081497ce237).
Hardware results: objective gate passed; corrected weight-sync gate **1 passed in
159.61 seconds**, Iris succeeded.

comments.author: atqamar-agent
comments.body:
🤖 **Give async execution its own timing and work accounting**

The observability mandate was to diagnose where time and generated work go while
many rollouts overlap. Summing overlapping rollout walls into a synchronous
“generate” phase would produce misleading timings.

We added per-call rollout timing, concurrent wait counters, queue/dwell/staleness
observations, group/token outcomes, event-loop lag, and explicit policy drains and
weight-sync phases. Policy drains measure waits for policy workers to reach
a synchronization point. Megatron received worker-side phase timing. Signed residuals
(parent wall minus exclusive child phases) expose accounting errors; process, rank,
step, and attempt identities keep unrelated observations separate.

CPU serialization, failure, concurrency, and accounting checks passed. The resulting
telemetry can distinguish useful consumed work from speculative work that is discarded.

Next at this milestone: verify the emitted records manually against actual training runs.

Evidence: [rollout observations](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/blob/001f6691aec4ee3beb16d2d82feac6eea73fd5eb/skyrl-train/skyrl_train/rollout_observability.py#L182);
[Megatron implementation](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/blob/001f6691aec4ee3beb16d2d82feac6eea73fd5eb/skyrl-train/skyrl_train/workers/megatron/megatron_worker.py).

comments.author: atqamar-agent
comments.body:
🤖 **Complete the synchronous end-to-end control**

The first full-run mandate was to establish a reproducible control through Marin:
regional input preparation, training, checkpointing, HF export, and evaluation.

The pinned fixture contained 1,024 training and 128 validation rows with disjoint
source IDs. Startup attempts exposed attention-backend and microbatch constraints;
we selected the supported fused-attention path and matched forward/train microbatches.
The successful control used eight policy and eight inference H100s.

It completed four optimizer updates and export/evaluation. Manual Finelog checks
verified **1,024 consumed sequences and 159,233 generated = consumed tokens**, with
all seven Megatron phases on all eight policy ranks at all four steps. This proved
the full pipeline; a remaining W&B terminal-state defect became the next task.

Next at this milestone: make tracker and process lifecycle equally reliable for sync and async.

Evidence: [sync control in W&B](https://wandb.ai/dogml/marin-async-non-agentic-rl/runs/n7wtf7vi).
This historical tracker later showed `crashed` despite successful Iris training;
the following milestone addresses that discrepancy.

comments.author: atqamar-agent
comments.body:
🤖 **Make W&B and Finelog agree on steps and completion**

Step-level W&B tracking was a requirement alongside Finelog, with the entity supplied
by launch configuration rather than hardcoded in the experiment.

We fixed shared-mode W&B logging to use an explicit global-step axis, commit each
training step, and finish with the training exit status. Investigation also found
that the async entrypoint bypassed the common experiment lifecycle, leaving worker
timings visible while trainer telemetry was missing. It now uses the shared lifecycle,
and evaluation scalars are mirrored into Finelog.

Success and failure lifecycle regressions passed. The corrected async runs subsequently
had **finished W&B histories with steps 1–4**, matching direct Finelog queries.

Next at this milestone: qualify the complete async pipeline under two freshness settings.

Evidence: [tracker implementation](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/blob/001f6691aec4ee3beb16d2d82feac6eea73fd5eb/skyrl-train/skyrl_train/utils/tracking.py#L93);
[lifecycle repair](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/commit/534dc5d2bb77d6c9e198754bbef24f99c7045e4e).

comments.author: atqamar-agent
comments.body:
🤖 **Complete async smokes with staleness limits 1 and 0**

The mandate was to establish real async functionality and freshness accounting,
before claiming performance. We ran matched four-update configurations with allowed
staleness 1 and 0, measured in completed policy updates; both completed training,
checkpoint/export, and terminal evaluation.
Each consumed **1,024 sequences** on 16 H100s.

| Token ledger | Staleness limit 1 | Staleness limit 0 |
|---|---:|---:|
| Generated response tokens | 195,522 | 158,043 |
| Consumed response/loss tokens | 158,148 | 158,043 |
| Discarded response tokens | 37,374 | 0 |

Both ledgers reconciled, observed consumed lag respected the configured bound, and
no nonfinite training values or telemetry loss were reported. A stale terminal queue
gauge exposed by this audit was then fixed and regression-tested.

Neither rollout completions nor recorded model-await intervals overlapped the
measured optimizer-training intervals in the small workload. Replacement generation
finished during learner preparation, before the optimizer phase. This describes the
recorded driver intervals; these functional smokes did not establish a speedup or
learning-quality result.

Next at this milestone: make these measurements easy to inspect and compare over longer sessions.

Evidence: [staleness-1 run](https://wandb.ai/dogml/marin-async-non-agentic-rl/runs/gl4sy92i),
[staleness-0 run](https://wandb.ai/dogml/marin-async-non-agentic-rl/runs/bjm39ire);
[queue-gauge repair](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/commit/663d88d20f71c6b0ac4fe1be586c76772b54c7ac).

comments.author: atqamar-agent
comments.body:
🤖 **Put real async telemetry in Grafana**

The dashboard mandate was a companion to Marin’s existing synchronous RL view,
with enough detail to diagnose the async producer/consumer relationship.

We added **Async RL Training**, initially with 21 panels covering progress, useful
work, queues, waits, staleness, policy/weight timings, overlap, quality, rank detail,
and exporter health. Filters preserve run/job/execution identity, and missing or
window-clipped observations remain distinguishable from measured zero.

The initial dashboard passed **77 SQL/provisioning tests**. Every panel and query
selector was also executed against live Finelog, and browser checks confirmed real
run data. Production deployment has not been performed.

Next at this milestone: extend the view with policy-probability drift and resource-normalized throughput.

Evidence: [dashboard source](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/3febf6b056f2a7903210dc91bc15f72fd3f1fe39/infra/grafana/dashboards/async_rl.json#L1).

comments.author: atqamar-agent
comments.body:
🤖 **Measure off-policy distance and useful work per resource**

The next mandate was to separate two questions: how many policy versions old is a
rollout, and how differently does the learner score the actual sampled tokens?

We added full-batch diagnostics for **pre-update learner logprob minus reported
behavior logprob** on finite loss tokens: coverage, signed/absolute log-ratio summaries,
tails, clipping-window pressure, and token-weight concentration. These reuse the
existing learner forward. We also added topology/batch metadata and consumed-token
rates normalized by configured policy/inference GPU counts. Core time excludes
callbacks; cycle time includes checkpoint/evaluation work up to metric publication.
Both exclude startup, epoch cleanup, and final export.

The dashboard grew to **29 panels**, with the new scalars also in W&B and Finelog.
Direct queries verified real values. A zero-version-lag Qwen batch still had mean
absolute log-ratio **0.01198**. This is a scoring discrepancy even without policy
aging; inference/training numerical differences are possible contributors whose
individual effects have not been isolated. These diagnostic ratios are not a KL
estimate or an established safe staleness threshold.

Next at this milestone: test their behavior across 100 updates and repeated epoch transitions.

Evidence: [drift calculation](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/blob/001f6691aec4ee3beb16d2d82feac6eea73fd5eb/skyrl-train/skyrl_train/utils/importance_ratio_diagnostics.py#L27),
[resource/time denominators](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/blob/001f6691aec4ee3beb16d2d82feac6eea73fd5eb/skyrl-train/skyrl_train/rollout_observability.py#L45),
[Qwen measurements](https://wandb.ai/dogml/marin-async-non-agentic-rl/runs/t4mom8ql).

comments.author: atqamar-agent
comments.body:
🤖 **Qualify a 100-update Qwen session**

The endurance mandate was to move beyond startup smokes while retaining the simple
Qwen/GSM8K, Megatron, eight-policy/eight-inference configuration.

The run completed **100 optimizer updates, syncs at updates 0–100, six epoch transitions,
and 25,600 consumed sequences**. Checkpoints ran every 25 updates and evaluation
every 10. Training, final HF export, and the separate terminal evaluation all succeeded;
W&B finished with all 100 training rows manually verified.

Finelog reconciled **6,690,949 generated tokens = 6,536,199 consumed + 154,750 discarded**.
All steps had finite drift diagnostics and one optimizer update, consumed lag remained
within 1, and the final queue was empty with no reported exporter loss.

This establishes a working longer-session baseline. Answers grew longer late in
training, and callback/epoch overhead remained visible, so endurance alone does not
establish an optimal resource split or an async speed advantage.

Next at this milestone: run a controlled 20-update sync/async comparison and qualify Snowball separately.

Evidence: [finished Qwen100 run](https://wandb.ai/dogml/marin-async-non-agentic-rl/runs/t4mom8ql);
[qualification schedule](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/3febf6b056f2a7903210dc91bc15f72fd3f1fe39/experiments/post_training/async_rl.py#L99).

comments.author: atqamar-agent
comments.body:
🤖 **Establish the first matched sync/async timing result**

The comparison mandate was to measure whether async completes equivalent training
work faster. Both arms used the same source, initial Qwen checkpoint, 1,536-row
fixture, optimizer/batch settings, seed, and **8 policy + 8 inference H100s** in the
same cluster. Each update consumed 64 prompts × 4 responses = 256 sequences.
Twenty updates stayed within one epoch, with evaluation/checkpointing only at update
20. Dispatch order and sampled trajectories can still differ.

We measured from initial weight sync through sync after update 20,
including rollout fill and interstep overhead, excluding setup and final callbacks.

| Measurement | Sync | Async |
|---|---:|---:|
| Optimizer updates / consumed sequences | 20 / 5,120 | 20 / 5,120 |
| Training-window time | 252.7 s | 320.8 s |
| Consumed response/loss tokens | 823,760 | 819,746 |
| Consumed tokens per second | 3,259.8 | 2,555.6 |
| Allocated GPU-hours in that window | 1.123 | 1.426 |

Async took **26.9% longer** and delivered **21.6% fewer consumed tokens per GPU-hour**.
Token counts differed by only 0.49%, and excluding the first two updates preserved
the finding. Both trackers finished with complete, finite step metrics.

The scheduled 128-example evaluation at update 20 scored **87/128 for sync and
79/128 for async**. A separate training-end callback repeated evaluation at the same
weights and also favored sync (89/128 versus 78/128). This single stochastic pair
does not establish a general quality effect. Both arms also completed HF export and
the separate terminal evaluation stage.

This is a useful calibration point for the epic: the current small-model configuration
has measurable overhead to address. It does not determine Snowball’s result or the
performance/quality tradeoff at other resource and freshness settings.

Next at this milestone: identify the costs behind the gap before changing GPU allocation.

Evidence: [sync run](https://wandb.ai/dogml/marin-async-non-agentic-rl/runs/xopx415q),
[async run](https://wandb.ai/dogml/marin-async-non-agentic-rl/runs/276c1nmj);
[comparison preset](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/3febf6b056f2a7903210dc91bc15f72fd3f1fe39/experiments/post_training/async_rl.py#L99).

comments.author: atqamar-agent
comments.body:
🤖 **Explain the measured weight-sync bottleneck**

The follow-up mandate was to distinguish weight communication from the other work
inside the synchronization timer.

In the 20-update pair, weight sync cost **48.79 seconds for sync versus
147.40 seconds for async**, including **100.55 seconds of async pause time**.
The client unconditionally waits five seconds before pausing inference schedulers.
Meanwhile, sync’s entire generation phase cost only **35.87 seconds** across the run.
Async’s admission wait totaled 1.96 seconds: a 33.91-second reduction relative to
sync generation. Weight sync added 98.61 seconds, and the combined learner/logprob
phases added 0.56 seconds. These separately measured components account for 65.27
of the 68.06-second slowdown. The pause is already included in weight-sync time.
This finding does not establish a slower network.

Weight sync happens after each optimizer update: Megatron reconstructs model
parameters and sends them **trainer → inference**, one parameter at a time. Gradients
and rollout logprobs are outside this transfer. The Qwen transfer crosses the policy/
inference node boundary; its retained logs do not establish the selected NCCL transport.

We also identified synchronous DataLoader worker startup at evaluation/epoch boundaries,
matching recurring ~30-second event-loop stalls, and duplicate final evaluation from
two callbacks. These sit outside the comparison’s primary timing window. Precise loader
cost attribution still needs dedicated timing.

Next at this milestone: test a correctness-preserving pause handshake, then rerun the control. Later
experiments can vary sync cadence, allowed lag, and GPU split; changing
`max_staleness_steps` alone currently does not change sync frequency.

Evidence: [pause implementation](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/blob/001f6691aec4ee3beb16d2d82feac6eea73fd5eb/skyrl-train/skyrl_train/inference_engines/inference_engine_client.py#L850),
[parameter sync](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/blob/001f6691aec4ee3beb16d2d82feac6eea73fd5eb/skyrl-train/skyrl_train/workers/megatron/megatron_worker.py#L739),
[DataLoader setup](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/blob/001f6691aec4ee3beb16d2d82feac6eea73fd5eb/skyrl-train/skyrl_train/utils/trainer_utils.py#L503),
[evaluation callbacks](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/blob/001f6691aec4ee3beb16d2d82feac6eea73fd5eb/skyrl-train/skyrl_train/callbacks/builtin.py#L149).

comments.author: atqamar-agent
comments.body:
🤖 **Prepare and launch the first Snowball qualification gate**

The next-model mandate is Megatron training of Snowball, the 67B-A2B mixture-of-experts
model, followed by sufficiently long runs to study resource balance and off-policy
tradeoffs.

We added separate two-update and 25-update presets around the existing regional
67B-A2B SFT export. The policy uses **32 H100s** with tensor parallelism 1, pipeline parallelism 2, and
expert parallelism 8; inference uses another **8 H100s** on one node. The export’s thinking template is retained, and host-memory/
disk requests account for Megatron checkpoint staging.

A regional CPU audit passed on all **1,024 training and 128 validation prompts** using
the actual export tokenizer: training prompts were 113–261 tokens, validation prompts
115–216. Both configurations passed full launcher/trainer validation. After capacity
became available, the **40-H100 two-update gate was admitted**. NCCL initialization
logging is enabled to inspect transport selection.

This milestone is model/configuration readiness and a launched gate. Snowball training
and the 25-update run are **not yet qualified**.

Next at this milestone: verify forward/backward, useful rewards, weight sync and subsequent
rollouts, checkpoint/export, and output-limit behavior before launching the longer run.

Evidence: [Snowball recipe and tokenizer audit](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/3febf6b056f2a7903210dc91bc15f72fd3f1fe39/experiments/post_training/async_snowball.py#L83).
Iris coordinator: `/atqamar/async-rl-snowball-gate-coordinator-v1`.

comments.author: atqamar-agent
comments.body:
🤖 Snowball completes two async updates

Snowball 67B-A2B now completes two async Megatron updates on 32 learner + 8 rollout H100s, including weight sync and checkpoint saving. [W&B](https://wandb.ai/dogml/marin-async-non-agentic-rl/runs/gxwqg87k) is finished with both steps recorded.

The first attempt exposed a gradient-buffer restore without a preceding offload. We replaced the manual storage handling with Megatron's native buffer lifecycle and rejected the unsupported async optimizer-offload setting. A one-H100 numerical regression passed before repeating the Snowball gate. [Repair](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/commit/e59c2e90bfb6a9664304ad13a760e6da55ceec1a).

The run consumed 256 responses and 127,786 tokens. Finelog reconciles 191,440 generated tokens = 127,786 consumed + 63,654 discarded at shutdown. Consumed weight-version lag was zero at update 1 and one at update 2; the recorded probability diagnostics were finite throughout.

Three observations set the next experiment:

- 81.25% of consumed responses at update 1 and 82.03% at update 2 hit the 512-token limit, with complete stop-reason coverage. The next run uses the planned 2,048-token per-response limit and measures this fraction again. Length stops alone do not establish answer incompleteness.
- Update 2 took 31.17 seconds of core training time, including 19.84 seconds of weight synchronization (63.6%) and about 4 milliseconds waiting for rollouts. Two updates are insufficient to choose a GPU split; longer Snowball measurements come first.
- Final checkpoint saving added about 554 seconds. We will report core throughput and checkpoint-inclusive completion time separately.

The new consumed-length metrics reached W&B but were omitted by Finelog's scalar filter. That filter is fixed for subsequent runs, and the Grafana dashboard now has a length-stop/coverage panel. Historical missing values remain gaps.

Automated export is currently blocked by Iris marking the head pod deleted after its successful driver exit. Next: recover conversion of the saved checkpoint to Hugging Face format, completing the model artifact needed by downstream consumers. Then start a fresh 25-update run from the original SFT model, evaluating the same held-out set before training and at update 25. This gate establishes training functionality; it does not establish a quality gain, a speed advantage, or the optimal allocation.

comments.author: atqamar-agent
comments.body:
🤖 Snowball checkpoint export completes; 25-update qualification submitted

The checkpoint from Snowball’s two-update gate now loads and exports successfully. Export-only recovery on 32 H100s finished all four tasks with exit 0, zero failures and zero preemptions, followed by portable HF artifact verification. This recovers the artifact; the original training coordinator’s completion failure remains a separate orchestration result.

An earlier recovery attempt exposed a scaling problem: each of 32 policy workers would download the entire 939 GB checkpoint. Staging once per node reduced that to four validated copies. Each contained 45 objects and 939.3 GB, taking 17.6–19.1 minutes per node. The successful export tasks took about 33 minutes overall. This checkpoint/export cost sits outside the training-update timing window. The repair is in [MSR133bb554](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/commit/133bb5541eb61c2f65f077195ee907efc38fe144), pinned by [Marin8250cfb3e1](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/commit/8250cfb3e1d92726028052da418f74dbb24f90fc).

Decision: proceed to 25-update Snowball qualification. The coordinator is submitted as `async-rl-snowball25-coordinator-v1` after checking H100 capacity. It starts from the original SFT model, uses 32 learner + 8 rollout GPUs, raises the response limit to 2,048 tokens, and evaluates the same 128 held-out prompts before and after training. Checkpointing remains at the final update because the gate’s save took roughly nine minutes. The next result should establish whether training and telemetry remain stable over longer responses and identify the next resource-allocation or weight-sync-schedule experiment. It does not yet establish an optimal GPU split or an acceptable policy-lag range.

comments.author: atqamar-agent
comments.body:
🤖 Snowball completes 25 async updates; sync cadence is the next control

Snowball completed 25 async Megatron updates on 32 learner + 8 rollout H100s, using GSM8K, GRPO, and a 2,048-token response limit. All five training tasks exited successfully with no retries or preemptions. [W&B](https://wandb.ai/dogml/marin-async-non-agentic-rl/runs/vupc3ir9) is finished with 25 finite training rows; direct Finelog queries verified syncs at updates 0–25, an empty terminal rollout buffer, and zero reported telemetry loss.

| Measurement | Result |
|---|---:|
| Core training-loop time, all 25 updates | 948.3 s |
| Updates 2–25: weight sync / training / rollout waiting | 56.2% / 21.9% / 21.4% of their 866.5 s core time |
| Final checkpoint saving | 547.3 s, outside core time |
| Consumed responses / response tokens | 3,200 / 3,312,485 |
| Generated tokens discarded as stale / terminal surplus | 7.52% / 3.32% |
| Consumed responses reaching the token limit | 17.44% |

The generated-token ledger closes exactly: 3,715,171 = 3,312,485 consumed + 279,441 stale + 123,245 terminal surplus. Core timing excludes evaluation, checkpointing, startup, and export; it is not the complete job runtime.

On the same 128 held-out prompts, greedy evaluation rose from 99/128 (77.3%) initially to 116/128 (90.6%) at update 25. The existing shutdown path repeated evaluation with the same final weights and scored 117/128 (91.4%). Keep these as two observations of the same checkpoint, without pooling them. This establishes a completed 25-update baseline; it does not establish a safe range of policy lag.

Consumed policy age stayed within one optimizer update. The token importance-weight ESS fraction stayed between 0.9909 and 0.9930; this drift diagnostic does not replace held-out evaluation.

Next, add a controlled weight-sync interval, preserving separate learner and installed-weight identities and measuring lag in optimizer updates. Validate the current every-update behavior, then gate an every-two-updates run before a matched 25-update comparison. Hold the other training and inference settings fixed, with a consistent initial/final evaluation schedule. Weight sync dominates the measured loop, so this is the next performance/quality experiment. A 16-learner-GPU control still needs a memory and full-update gate. vLLM optimization remains in its separate workstream.

Snowball completed the instrumented two-update gate on 32 learner + 8 rollout H100s with a 4,096-token response cap and 8,192-token context. The training job and coordinator succeeded. A separate CPU audit verified the durable training result, finished [W&B history](https://wandb.ai/dogml/marin-async-non-agentic-rl/runs/ixw8mr27), and no checkpoint/export artifacts. Finelog recorded both updates with finite drift diagnostics, zero reported telemetry loss, and an empty terminal buffer. The token ledger balances: 303,755 generated = 272,643 consumed + 31,112 terminal surplus.

The new allocator telemetry produced 480 observations covering all 32 learner GPUs:

| Measurement | Maximum across learner GPUs |
|---|---:|
| Model-ready allocated memory, before lazy optimizer state | 35.3 GiB |
| Learner logprob-forward allocated peak | 53.8 GiB |
| PPO forward/backward/update allocated peak | 56.6 GiB |
| Weight-sync allocated peak / reserved peak | 58.1 / 61.5 GiB |

These are PyTorch allocator measurements; reserved bytes include cache. Device free memory is sampled at phase boundaries, and initialization/checkpoint/export peaks are outside this coverage. They should not be equated with W&B's whole-device memory usage.

Decision: retain 32 learner GPUs for the next experiments. Halving the learner allocation with the same TP1/PP2/EP8 layout would add roughly 23.4 GiB per rank in persistent state. Combining that increase with the observed weight-sync footprint would exceed these H100s' capacity before accounting for allocations outside PyTorch. The dashboard now has 33 data panels, including memory by phase, inference service rates aligned with learner phases, and core GPU-hours. Direct queries verified all three on this run. Service rates show sample coverage and exclude counter resets and intervals crossing phase boundaries. Core time was 111.6 seconds, or 1.24 configured GPU-hours; startup and shutdown are excluded. This gate does not estimate instrumentation overhead or establish a speedup.

Re-querying Snowball25 updates 2–25 further narrows the weight-sync bottleneck: each sync averaged 20.30 seconds, comprising 5.18 seconds pausing generation and 15.09 seconds in the broadcast path. The two outer drain barriers together averaged 22 milliseconds. Broadcast includes extraction, conversion, receiver loading and per-parameter barriers, so its 41.8% share of core time is not pure network time.

Next: the five-update cadence-2 gate is submitted after a fresh H100 capacity check, with initial/final evaluation and a forced sync at update 5. Then run the response-budget pilots and matched cadence controls.
