comments.body:
🤖 Response-budget pilots make stale rollout work a priority

Two Snowball async pilots completed 25 updates each on 32 learner + 8 rollout H100s. Both used weight sync every update, allowed age of one completed learner update, an 8,192-token context, a common 4,096-token evaluation cap, four rollouts per training prompt, and completion without checkpoint saving or HF export. The training response cap was the changed parameter.

| Measurement | 2,048-token cap | 4,096-token cap |
|---|---:|---:|
| Core RL time | 914.4 s | 1,202.4 s |
| Consumed response tokens | 3,139,919 | 3,629,028 |
| Length-limit stops / 3,200 responses | 467 (14.6%) | 116 (3.6%) |
| Generated tokens rejected as stale | 1.4% | 32.9% |
| Core time waiting for usable rollouts | 18.6% | 37.6% |
| Initial → final correct evaluation answers / 128 | 104 → 120 | 100 → 116 |

The larger-cap run reduced truncation and took 31.5% longer in core time, while consuming 15.6% more tokens. The difference was concentrated in buffer waiting (+281.6 s); learner training and sync totals each changed by under 1.5 s. Its token ledger closes exactly: 5,807,538 generated = 3,629,028 consumed + 1,910,321 stale + 268,189 surplus tokens discarded during termination. The exclusive weight-sync phase occupied 42.5% of core time, versus 55.7% with the smaller cap; it excludes the reported rollout-wait phase.

Both Iris coordinators and all GPU tasks succeeded. Independent W&B and storage audits verified 25 finite update records, durable results confirming update 25, and no saved checkpoints or HF weights. Direct Finelog queries verified both ledgers, empty terminal buffers and zero reported telemetry loss. [2,048-token W&B](https://wandb.ai/dogml/marin-async-non-agentic-rl/runs/znzcxidg), [4,096-token W&B](https://wandb.ai/dogml/marin-async-non-agentic-rl/runs/n538941o).

Neither cap is a demonstrated quality winner. Initial evaluation differed despite common settings; both improved by a net 16 correct answers. The 128-prompt development set and one run per cap are insufficient for a quality-equivalence claim. These concurrent pilots also do not exclude shared-fabric contention. Core time excludes startup, evaluation and teardown; configured core GPU-hours were 10.16 and 13.36.

Decision: use 4,096 tokens provisionally for the next controls to reduce truncation, retaining 2,048 as a cheaper reference. Qualify admission and sync cadence before adding inference GPUs: stale work and weight sync are both substantial. The [prior memory measurements](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/8936#issuecomment-5558104237), including 56.6 GiB during PPO and 58.1 GiB during weight sync, support retaining 32 learner GPUs; halving that allocation requires a different memory plan.

A subsequent gate of the new sync-aware admission implementation exposed a correctness race after update 2: new requests were released while inference was still paused. Fixing and requalifying that boundary precedes the matched Snowball sync/async and cadence controls. Frozen-weight evaluation repeatability will precede reward-margin claims. Two independent inference replicas, each with eight-way expert parallelism on one node, remain the first allocation arm after those controls.

Sources: [MarinSkyRL 4a763d35](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/commit/4a763d358ff23980ab10b8fbb451907c574ac7c5), [Marin cfed1163de](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/commit/cfed1163de13aa501b115215f91a3b3c5053aba6).

The matched 25-update Qwen screen is complete and independently audited in W&B, durable receipts and Finelog. All arms used the same pinned model/data/source, seed 17, 64 prompts × four responses, 1,024-token output cap, no KL, and 8 learner + 8 inference H100s.

| Arm | Core RL time | Consumed response tokens | Final development score |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Sync | 250.5s | 1,147,575 | 80/128 |
| Async C1/A1 | 339.5s | 1,055,680 | 75/128 |
| Async C2/A1 | 256.4s | 1,040,896 | 84/128 |

C denotes sync interval; A is permitted consumed update age. C2 reduced core time by **24.5% relative to C1**. Weight-sync time fell from **184.3s to 95.8s**, including pause time from 125.8s to 65.4s. The training phase remained approximately 143s in both async arms; buffer waiting increased from 3.0s to 12.6s. These phase measurements explain most of the difference. C2 was still 2.3% slower than sync and consumed 9.3% fewer tokens: this is not an equal-work speedup claim.

The exposure measurements also matter: 92% of C1 prompt groups were age 1, versus 48% for C2. All 75 updates had complete finite behavior-probability coverage. C2's largest early drift event had mean squared log-ratio 0.01544 and token-weight ESS fraction 0.99149, then subsided. Age 0/sync measurements retain a nonzero likelihood-mismatch floor, so version age and probability drift are complementary diagnostics.

Snowball's matched 25 sync/C1/C2 block is already running; its resource decision remains model-specific.

These concurrent, single-seed runs are screening evidence. They share data configuration but not sampled trajectories or exact consumed ordering; the 25-update Qwen horizon crosses an epoch boundary. Initial development scores were 7/7/6 out of 128, and initial response hashes differed even where scores matched. The final scores therefore do not establish a quality winner. Frozen-weight evaluation repeats are running separately; larger untouched evaluation, training seeds and controlled timing repetitions precede final recommendations.

comments.body:
🤖 Qwen diagnostics qualify the next Snowball and off-policy experiments

Two four-update Qwen runs completed cleanly, with identical configuration except the optional wire-weight survey. Each repeated evaluation three times before training began. Independent CPU audits verified W&B, receipts, all ten evaluation dumps, ordered prompt identities and token hashes.

**Evaluation has measurable variation at fixed weights.** Startup scores were 8/7/7 out of 128 with the observer off and 6/7/8 with it on. Within a run, paired passes changed reward on 1–5 prompts and output tokens on 20–57 prompts. All 128 prompts retained their logical engine indices and source order. This demonstrates repeat variation; it does not identify its numerical cause or attribute it to the observer. Small single-run reward differences remain insufficient for selecting a quality winner.

**Sparse weight sync now has a measured reason for further investigation.** The survey covered the full Qwen converted-wire inventory: 311 tensors and 1.503 GB per dense weight sync. Stratified exact-bit samples estimated that **1.18–1.93% of transmitted BF16 elements changed** across updates 1–4. A hypothetical tensor-local uint32 index plus replacement value would occupy **3.53–5.78% of the dense payload**, before headers, encoding and application. These are sampled weight-change estimates; no compression codec or transfer speedup has been demonstrated.

The observer pair took 61.65s off versus 62.92s on in core RL, with sync totals of 29.34s versus 30.62s. Capture cost was about 0.19s per sync. The short concurrent pair does not precisely identify observer overhead; capture/CUDA/comparison timings overlap and must not be added. The survey and coverage fields are now available in the async Grafana dashboard.

**The existing regular-PPO + capped-TIS objective also passed its numerical gate.** On eight H100s, real Megatron Qwen workers matched an independently calculated scalar/gradient oracle through a nonzero optimizer update and post-update log probabilities. The exact test passed in 104.95s; the Iris job completed successfully. This qualifies objective wiring, not a reward benefit.

Decisions: carry frozen evaluation and the bounded wire survey to Snowball before considering a codec; run the Qwen C1/A3 allowance comparison before selecting a correction experiment. Both proceed independently of Snowball's matched 25-update timing controls. For longer cross-scheduler studies, an opt-in shared epoch-seeded source order is being qualified: current async repeats its initial permutation while sync advances it. Existing results retain that documented behavior.

Runs: [observer off](https://wandb.ai/dogml/marin-async-non-agentic-rl/runs/d2sa5fj1), [observer on](https://wandb.ai/dogml/marin-async-non-agentic-rl/runs/8105hbfb). comments.author: atqamar-agent
comments.body:
🤖 Snowball timing controls justify testing a second inference replica

All three Snowball 67B-A2B runs on GSM8K completed 25 updates cleanly. Independent W&B and storage audits verified the actual attempts, finite step metrics, receipts and six evaluation dumps; Finelog verified token accounting and terminal telemetry. Each used 32 learner + 8 inference H100s, the same model/data/source, seed 17, 32 prompts × four responses, a 4,096-token response cap and an 8,192-token context, without KL, checkpoints or HF export.

| Arm | Core RL time | Consumed response tokens | Task-running GPU-hours | Development score, initial → final |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Sync | 1,652.8s | 3,829,716 | 24.87 | 96 → 120/128 |
| Async, sync every update (C1) | 1,182.2s | 3,678,622 | 21.02 | 99 → 116/128 |
| Async, sync every two updates (C2) | 959.7s | 3,787,815 | 19.00 | 98 → 117/128 |

Core RL time sums collection/waiting, learner computation and weight sync across updates; it excludes startup, evaluation and teardown. The development score counts correct answers among 128 questions. Both async arms permit consumed data to lag the learner by at most one completed update, measured from the policy used to generate it. C2 can train once more between syncs while remaining within that bound. C1 used 28.5% less core time than sync, with 3.9% fewer consumed tokens. C2 used 41.9% less time than sync, with 1.1% fewer tokens; that comparison includes the sync-cadence change. These concurrent, single-seed runs measure whole-runner behavior, with different sampled trajectories and completion ordering. They do not isolate overlap or exclude shared-fabric contention.

Within async, C2 reduced weight-sync time from 511.7s to 267.6s while learner training remained approximately 232s. Its token ledger closes exactly: 3,972,064 generated = 3,787,815 consumed + 184,249 terminal surplus, with zero stale discards. C1 discarded 1,387,902 stale tokens; this is an observed difference between the runs, without an isolated explanation of its full size. With C2, waiting for usable rollouts now takes 455.4s, or 47.5% of core time. The next allocation experiment tests whether additional inference capacity reduces that waiting.

The allocation and token budget came from successive constraints: 32 learner GPUs were initially a feasible training geometry; the measured 56.6 GiB PPO and 58.1 GiB weight-sync peaks supported retaining it. This block reconfirmed peaks of 56.69/58.11 GiB. Eight inference GPUs formed one node-local expert-parallel replica. The earlier 2,048-token baseline was increased provisionally to 4,096 after the token-budget pilots reduced length-limit stops. None of those starting choices established an optimal ratio.

Next: verify physical GPU placement, weight delivery and five training updates with 32 learner + 16 inference GPUs as two independent node-local replicas, then compare allocations at fixed C2 cadence and token limits. At 48 GPUs, core time must fall below 799.8s to improve core GPU-hours over the current 40-GPU result. We will also compare task-running GPU-hours, calculated from each Iris task's start/finish times; the table includes setup, evaluation and teardown, excludes pre-running queue time, and is not a billing measure.

Final scores are observations on the reused 128-question development set, not evidence of quality equivalence. Frozen-weight repeats, longer training, repeated seeds and untouched evaluation remain required for the drift/time/reward study. Parallel diagnostics measure how increasing Qwen’s permitted data age changes actual drift, and how many Snowball weight elements change between syncs.

Runs: [sync](https://wandb.ai/dogml/marin-async-non-agentic-rl/runs/v41mx02h), [async C1](https://wandb.ai/dogml/marin-async-non-agentic-rl/runs/aiufq217), [async C2](https://wandb.ai/dogml/marin-async-non-agentic-rl/runs/vtu41g4d). Sources: [MarinSkyRL 29f7b923](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/commit/29f7b92376ca403489a6d76777a46badfdce2c7c), [Marin 1a4a9bcb8a](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/commit/1a4a9bcb8a0f2064fa61b2a84635b626cf9f664f).

comments.author: atqamar-agent
comments.body:
🤖 Qwen cadence cuts weight-sync overhead and advances to longer drift testing

The new shared-source-order Qwen controls completed cleanly and passed independent W&B, durable-result and Finelog audits. All used Qwen3-0.6B, GSM8K, seed 17, 64 prompts × four responses, 8 learner + 8 inference H100s, a 1,024-token response cap and no KL. C is the sync interval in optimizer updates; A is the maximum permitted consumed update age.

Increasing the age allowance alone was insufficient: C1/A1 and C1/A3 took 336.2s and 336.1s over 25 updates. A3 did change exposure—84% of consumed prompt groups were age 2—but did not shorten core time. This motivated changing sync cadence at that allowance.

| 25-update arm | Core RL time | Consumed response tokens | Weight-sync time | Token-weighted mean squared log-ratio | Minimum token-weight ESS fraction |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| C1/A3, behavior clipping | 336.1s | 1,014,965 | 183.5s | 0.002323 | 0.9960 |
| C4/A3, behavior clipping | 207.5s | 1,019,420 | 51.3s | 0.003568 | 0.9613 |

C4 used **38.3% less core time and delivered 1.63× consumed-token throughput**, with token counts within 0.5%. Syncs occurred at updates 0/4/8/12/16/20/24/25; the forced final sync is included in core time. Realized ages spanned 0–3, with finite behavior-probability coverage and zero admission rejections. Here the log-ratio compares learner and rollout token log-probabilities. The probability-drift and effective-sample-size measurements show that this speed gain comes with different off-policy exposure.

Both arms ended at 76/128 on the reused development questions. That is not evidence of quality equivalence: this is one seed, startup scores differed, and frozen-weight evaluation repeats already showed output variation. Shared epoch-seeded source order now advances consistently across epochs; asynchronous completion still changes consumed ordering and sampled trajectories.

**Decision:** advance C1/A1 and C4/A3 to a matched 100-update development block. A third arm combines C4/A3 with the numerically qualified regular-PPO + truncated importance sampling (TIS, cap 2) objective, after a short combined gate. The C1/A3 TIS screen completed with no correction skips but did not improve timing, so the useful question is whether the correction package helps at C4's faster, mixed-age exposure. It is a comparison of objective packages, not an isolated estimate of TIS alone.

The longer block uses common evaluations at updates 0/20/40/60/80/100. Choosing an interval divisible by four avoids evaluation forcing extra off-grid weight syncs. comments.author: atqamar-agent
comments.body:
🤖 Sparse weight changes justify measurement, but the host codec fails the timing gate

We will keep the current host reconstruction codec out of production weight sync. Cadence and the controlled training study continue; a more complex cache and apply architecture is deferred.

The Snowball survey measured the actual converted weight bits sent to inference. Gradients are not sent on this channel. Across five consecutive syncs, sampled bit changes were 2.13–2.87% of a complete 502-tensor inventory containing 134,157,778,944 wire bytes, including FP32 router state. Each receiver gets the full wire tensor before its expert-parallel loader selects local ownership. A full predecessor cache would therefore require 124.94 GiB per receiver, about 1 TiB across an EP8 node if each receiver maintains an independent full cache.

The bounded replay reconstructed all 60 measured cases exactly on two H100s in one node. For 64 MiB of BF16 weights with 2% and 3% changed elements, indexed replacements used 6% and 9% of dense payload bytes. Median acknowledged elapsed times were 276.575 and 296.576 ms, versus 1.068 and 1.203 ms for resident-GPU dense transfer. CPU encoding and hashing, host/device copies, and reconstruction outweighed the payload savings.

This is a negative result for the tested host codec. It includes a full reconstructed-range copy back to the receiver GPU, even at zero changes; that cost is not a lower bound for a future in-place GPU design. The replay used synthetic chunks and exercised neither the Snowball loader nor inter-node InfiniBand. It does not establish a general result about compression.

Implementation: [bounded replay and exactness tests](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/commit/60643c0f96ef19b59f9aeca0f0738e768a0bdaf2). GPU evidence: 60 exact cases, BF16/FP32, 0/2/3/20/100% changes, three measured repetitions per case. No production transport was changed.

comments.body:
🤖 Snowball100: C4/A3 uses less time and GPU-hours; reward needs confirmation

Both 100-update async runs completed cleanly and passed independent W&B, durable-result and Finelog audits. Both used 32 learner + 8 inference H100s, the same Snowball export, seed 17, shared epoch-seeded source order, 32 prompts × 4 responses, 4,096-token training/evaluation caps and 8,192-token context. Evaluations were at 0/20/40/60/80/100; metrics-only completion skipped native checkpoints and HF export.

| Async configuration | Core RL seconds | Task-running GPU-hours | Consumed response tokens | Development initial → final /128 |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| [C2/A1 behavior clip](https://wandb.ai/dogml/marin-async-non-agentic-rl/runs/x3532fq8) | 4,025.678 | 57.289 | 18,971,098 | 98 → 120 |
| [C4/A3 behavior clip](https://wandb.ai/dogml/marin-async-non-agentic-rl/runs/fpsr78x8) | 2,313.578 | 38.237 | 13,561,656 | 104 → 117 |

Core RL time excludes startup and evaluation and includes final weight sync. C4/A3 reduced core time by **42.5%** and task-running GPU-hours by **33.3%**, while consuming **28.5% fewer tokens** at the same update/sequence budget. Consumed-token throughput improved 24.4% per core second and 7.1% per task-running GPU-hour. C is sync cadence and A is the maximum admitted group age in completed updates: this changes both controls within the async runner. It does not isolate generation/training overlap. Task-running GPU-hours include all GPU attempts' setup, evaluation and teardown, exclude pre-running reservations, and are not billing.

Weight-sync time fell from 1,079.7 to 529.4 seconds and buffer waiting from 2,085.2 to 949.5 seconds; learner training was nearly unchanged at 830.8 versus 813.0 seconds. The timing benefit therefore lies mainly in waiting and weight sync, alongside the changed rollout work.

The fixed update-100 development difference was C4−C2 **−2.34 percentage points**, with a question-paired 95% bootstrap interval of **[−6.25, +1.56] points**. The difference in initial-to-final gain was −7.03 points, interval [−16.41, +2.34]. These intervals condition on one training seed and reuse the 128 development questions. They leave a meaningful quality loss plausible; neither equal quality nor a quality winner is established.

All 200 updates had finite probability diagnostics and complete behavior-logprob coverage. Weight-sync schedules and admitted ages matched their configurations, token ledgers balanced, and terminal telemetry reported no queued or lost records. Mean squared learner/behavior log-ratio, weighted by consumed loss tokens, was 0.00690 for C2 and 0.00781 for C4. Minimum token-weight effective sample size (ESS) fractions were 0.9898 and 0.9843. These are measurements on each run's consumed tokens, including backend probability differences.

Two findings affect the next experiments. During updates 60–100, only about 12–13% of prompt groups had differing rewards across their four responses, limiting GRPO learning signal on this task set. Within C4, age-0 responses averaged 628 tokens and age-3 responses 1,733; informative-group fractions were 9.875% and 38.75%. The age-conditioned mean squared log-ratio was not monotonic. This is consistent with completion order selecting longer, less consistently solved groups into older batches. An observed age-versus-reward relationship cannot be attributed to staleness alone.

**Decision:** retain C2/A1 as the reference and complete one promoted C4/A3 correction candidate before selecting at most two configurations for confirmation. The regular-PPO + truncated importance sampling package (cap 2, required rollout logprobs) passed its five-update Snowball gate: syncs at updates 0/4/5, finite coverage, zero correction skips, exact work accounting and clean completion. Its matched [100-update run](https://wandb.ai/dogml/marin-async-non-agentic-rl/runs/ovmo3gnb) is now submitted. This changes an objective package; it is not an isolated estimate of importance sampling alone.

Confirmation keeps the fixed 100-update endpoint, uses seeds 17/29/43, and evaluates the disjoint 1,191-question GSM8K test window only at updates 0 and 100. Configurations will be frozen before confirmation launches or scores are read. The CPU data gate verified the row range, template and prompt bounds. Counterbalanced paired blocks and a serial block will check timing beyond this concurrent development screen. Harder tasks and an experiment isolating temporal age from completion order remain subsequent work.

Sources for this completed pair: [MarinSkyRL fb55d3bb](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/commit/fb55d3bb66fe96b7cb85ccfc313afe06a5386c02), [Marin 0e88be76](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/commit/0e88be76f8e364911a9d80cb440cc3f5086a7583). The Snowball correction control and paired auditor use [Marin 39b051cd](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/commit/39b051cd97d35c190c11e25160793543d3fcb5ab); the default recipe is unchanged. comments.body:
🤖 Evaluation audits expose rewarded repetition

The completed 100-update Snowball comparison has a quality distinction that raw GSM8K reward hides:

| Configuration | Raw correct /128 | Correct with completed stop /128 | Length-stopped /128 | Core seconds | Task-running GPU-hours |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| C2/A1 behavior clip | 120 | 64 | 63 | 4025.7 | 57.29 |
| C4/A3 behavior clip | 117 | 101 | 25 | 2313.6 | 38.24 |

A regional CPU audit reconstructed the original scores from saved tokens, text and ground truth. The verifier accepts the first `#### <answer>` match, including quoted matches inside thinking. Some rewarded responses repeat answer-format instructions until the cap. Neither configured EOS token appears inside the truncated responses; actual generation settings and token-aware checks provide no evidence of EOS being ignored. Repetition was already present in some initial-model responses, so this does not isolate its cause to cadence or the loss package.

A stricter final-line checker introduced its own misleading result: among rewarded, stopped C4 responses, the 77 it rejected were all correct answers in concluding prose, such as `The final answer is "#### 18".` C2's 41 stopped format failures differed: 40 continued after a valid answer line, and 37 contained generated role labels. Literal format compliance, mathematical correctness and completion must remain separate.

The importance-corrected Snowball arm is still running its fixed 100-update budget. At update 60 it scored 118/128, but 124 responses hit the cap and only four rewarded responses stopped. This is an interim generation-quality concern despite healthy finite probability diagnostics and zero skipped TIS corrections.

RJ's [curriculum experiments](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/8765#issuecomment-5523272145) provide a relevant caution: simply increasing the training token budget did not cure repetition/truncation or improve the composite result. We are preserving the scorer and the current run's parameters.

**Decision and next step:** evaluation work, stop coverage and reward contributions by stop class are now instrumented, independently audited, and represented in Grafana. Contributions use all evaluation responses as their denominator. Completed stopping is still not a general final-answer certificate. Finish the TIS arm, then explicitly review candidate selection using cost and completion evidence before any locked held-out scores are read; strict formatting will remain a diagnostic, not the primary quality score. The planned repeated-seed comparison will report raw reward and completion separately. These remain development results from reused questions and one training seed.

Sources: [MarinSkyRL evaluation metrics](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/commit/f38b7afdca2232f08b43d3934753273b0b442194), [Marin audit and dashboard](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/commit/67441401603573800969f0b3680394ac36caebc9).

This compares complete backend configurations. FSDP2 is configured for BF16 optimizer moments and gradient reduction, stochastic parameter updates, and different sharding; Megatron is configured for FP32 master weights, moments and gradient reduction. We cannot attribute the memory difference to one setting or infer that 16 learner GPUs would fit. Core RL time was 157.8 versus 162.2 seconds, with 704,679 versus 715,077 consumed tokens. These short runs overlapped other cluster work and do not establish a backend speed ranking or learning-quality equivalence. Initial and final 128-question response, reward and stop records were retained for quality analysis.

Next: keep the frozen Snowball cadence confirmation unchanged, and screen optimizer precision on Qwen with separate native-FP32, precision-aware-FP32 and lower-precision-state controls. First verify actual live state dtypes, update numerics and save/load continuation. Then measure persistent and peak memory, elapsed time, drift, reward and completion behavior before any Snowball promotion. The pinned optimizer can temporarily expand BF16 moments to FP32 during an update, so lower persistent storage alone is insufficient evidence of a lower peak.

comments.author: atqamar-agent
comments.body:
🤖 A qualified supplemental answer diagnostic unlocks the next Qwen comparison

The historical reward audits showed why raw correctness reward needs completion and answer-format context: a response can earn reward before it stops, or before it delivers a final answer. We have kept the original scorer unchanged and qualified a separate, versioned final-answer diagnostic using retained development responses. No held-out confirmation responses were used to tune it.

Two earlier parser candidates each falsely accepted one answer in fresh blind checks. The failures exposed an unresolved reconsideration tail and a truncated numbered list. After bounded fixes, the third candidate's fresh 48-case check found 21 extractions matching the blinded asserted-answer labels, nine abstentions on otherwise readable answers, and 18 abstentions due to answer or response-structure problems, with no false acceptance observed. Labels were frozen before revealing predictions; an independent comparison and six additional pre-key spotchecks agreed. The reviewer had prior study/parser context. This was a diagnostic, stratified sample, so it does not establish a population error rate. The conservative parser still misses some benign formats.

**Decision:** use this diagnostic alongside raw reward, accepted-stop completion, truncation, and extraction coverage. Do not count all abstentions as incorrect mathematics or replace the original reward with this parser's score.

**Next:** run six matched 100-update Qwen arms: sync/staleness settings C1/A1 and C4/A3, each crossed with behavior clipping, regular PPO without TIS, and regular PPO with capped TIS. This adds the missing reference+TIS arm and the regular-PPO controls needed to distinguish the correction from the objective change. All arms use the same model/data revisions, seed, topology, token limits, and evaluation schedule. The shared model/data preflight has passed; favorable contrasts require another training seed before Snowball promotion. Snowball's frozen confirmation runs continue independently.

comments.author: atqamar-agent
comments.body:
🤖 Snowball confirmation exposes unstable termination across seeds

The second seed of the frozen 100-update Snowball comparison completed and passed the W&B, receipt, Finelog, source, placement, and evaluation-integrity audits. C is the sync interval in optimizer updates; A is the maximum admitted group age in updates. Both configurations use 32 learner GPUs, eight inference GPUs, a 4,096-token response cap, and the same 1,191-question held-out evaluation window.

| Seed 29 arm | Core seconds | Task-running GPU-hours | Final raw reward count | Rewarded with accepted stop | Length-limited responses |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| C2/A1 | 3,594.8 | 57.61 | 1,088 | 374 | 809 |
| C4/A3 | 2,663.9 | 47.21 | 1,080 | 6 | 1,184 |

All quality counts use the same denominator of 1,191. Accepted-stop reward is a completion supplement, not a certificate of semantic final-answer correctness. C4 consumed 15.84 million response tokens versus C2's 12.29 million, so these are fixed-update results, not an equal-token comparison. Task-running GPU-hours include setup, evaluation and teardown; they exclude reservations before tasks started and are not a billing estimate. Other jobs shared the cluster.

The variation between these two seeds is material: C4's rewarded-and-stopped count was 510/1,191 in seed 17 and 6/1,191 in seed 29. High raw correctness reward therefore does not establish reliable completed answers. We have not attributed this behavior specifically to cadence, staleness, or another mechanism.

**Decision:** the C4 package, which had lower observed core time, is not established as a reliable operating default. Complete the predeclared third seed without changing configurations or selecting checkpoints, then report reward, termination, policy drift, elapsed time, token work, and GPU-hours together. For that serial reference/candidate block, finish our current Qwen and sparse-transfer jobs first and avoid our own additional east-cluster GPU experiments across both arms. External contention will still be recorded. The Qwen objective-control fleet continues to investigate the algorithm choices independently.

comments.author: atqamar-agent
comments.body:
🤖 Exact sparse weight updates reach inter-node replay without a clear timing gain

The GPU codecs now pass a two-host H100 replay over NCCL InfiniBand/GDRDMA. Both tasks completed cleanly, and all 720 two-rank transactions reconstructed the target bytes exactly. This tests changed weight values against an identified predecessor; production still sends dense weights.

| BF16 elements changed | Dense | 32-bit indices | Block-local 16-bit indices |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 2% | 14.344 ms | 14.085 ms | 14.522 ms |
| 3% | 14.807 ms | 15.230 ms | 14.738 ms |

Each entry is the median of three repeats of **eight verified transactions**: four serial 16 MiB chunks, with two successive versions each. The timing includes packing, control messages, full predecessor/target integrity checks, transfer, receiver installation and acknowledgement. Repeat ranges overlap. These are synthetic changed-bit patterns, not a whole-model weight-sync benchmark or trained Qwen/Snowball fixtures. The job allocated 16 H100s to obtain two hosts, used one GPU per host, and consumed 0.359 task-running GPU-hours. Source: MarinSkyRL `14ae698e`.

The earlier host codec was much slower than dense transfer. The GPU inter-node probe is close to its dense control, but the large byte reduction still did not produce a compelling end-to-end gain. Three preceding inter-node attempts failed during rendezvous/network initialization before benchmarking; those failures remain recorded separately.

**Decision:** do not integrate sparse weight sync yet. Next, capture bounded, predeclared contiguous windows of actual Qwen weights across successful syncs and replay their exact changes. Then test whether amortizing per-chunk control work helps, with identical integrity and acknowledgement obligations for dense and sparse variants. Record the additional staging memory and capture overhead. Snowball's serial confirmation continues independently.

comments.author: atqamar
comments.body:
🤖 **This epic closes here and continues as a structured program in `#8955`**

Everything built here is the base of the successor: the token-preserving async path,
sync cadence and sync-aware admission, drift and useful-work telemetry, the
Async RL Training dashboard, metrics-only completion with durable receipts, node-local inference
placement, one-copy-per-node checkpoint staging, and the paired-evaluation auditor.

## What we learned (numbers are from audited runs; details in the milestone comments above)

**Where the time goes.**
1. At Snowball scale, weight sync dominated async core time: 56% of a 25-update run, about
   20 s per sync, of which 15 s was the per-tensor broadcast and 5 s an unconditional pause
   grace. On Qwen3-0.6B the same 5 s pause was half of every 15 s step and explained the whole
   sync-vs-async gap (async 27% slower at 20 updates).
2. Syncing less often was the lever that moved: C2 cut Qwen core time 24%; C4 cut it 38–42% on
   both models at equal updates, and 33% in GPU-hours at 100 Snowball updates. Raising the
   admitted age alone (A1→A3) changed which groups were consumed (84% at age 2) but not the time.
3. A second inference replica (I16) bought 5.8% wall-clock at +17% GPU-hours. It is a time option,
   not an optimum.
4. The first cadence-2 gate admitted a cohort that could never be consumed (31% stale tokens); a
   sync-aware admission bound removed that entirely.

**What the reward was hiding.**
5. Raw GSM8K reward is not usable answer quality: the verifier accepts the first `#### n` anywhere,
   including inside thinking. Snowball C2 scored 120/128 raw with 64 completed answers; the TIS arm
   scored 113/128 with all 128 final responses cut off at the token cap. Report completed-stop
   reward and truncation with every raw number.
6. Nontermination predates TIS, develops between updates 25 and 100, and is seed-unstable: the
   same C4/A3 configuration completed 510 of 1,191 held-out answers at one seed and 6 at another.
   No configuration selected on raw reward survived that.
7. A strict "answer on the final line" check rejected 77 correct answers written in concluding
   prose. Format checks are diagnostics, never the score.
8. Evaluation at fixed weights is not repeatable at this scale (8/7/7 vs 6/7/8 of 128 on Qwen;
   97/102/101 on Snowball), so the 128-question dev set cannot separate arms closer than ~5–10.
9. GSM8K saturates for Snowball: after 60 updates only 12–13% of groups had mixed outcomes, so
   most rollout tokens carried no gradient.

**Levers that did not pay as tried.**
10. "TIS" was compared as an objective package (regular PPO + truncated IS vs behaviour-clip), so
    it did not isolate the correction; on Snowball it consumed 3× the tokens with no quality gain.
11. Sparse weight sync: only 1.2–1.9% (Qwen) and 2.1–2.9% (Snowball) of synced bf16 elements
    change per update, but the host codec was 250× slower than a dense copy and the GPU index
    codecs 24–33% slower on one host with no gain across nodes. The saving is real; the codec was
    the wrong place to look.
12. Memory: the default Megatron recipe needs 32 learner GPUs (56.7 GiB PPO peak, 58.1 GiB at
    weight sync). The optimized FSDP2 package peaked at 38.6 / 14.9 GiB, but it is a different
    precision package (bf16 optimizer state), so the difference is not attributable to sharding.

**Infrastructure lessons.**
13. Export downloaded a 939 GB checkpoint once per worker (32 copies) until staging became
    one copy per node (17–19 min per node).
14. An Iris head pod deleted after a clean exit marks the run failed; the receipt survives and is
    the record. Never auto-retry, never restart a cluster.
15. An inner direnv reset the W&B entity; an 8-worker spawned dataloader stalled the driver ~30 s
    at every eval and epoch reset; fair sync-vs-async comparisons needed a shared epoch-seeded
    prompt order. All three are now fixed or documented.
16. Every run's token ledger balanced (generated = consumed + stale + discarded) and every result
    was cross-audited across W&B, receipts and Finelog. That discipline carries over unchanged.

**Process lesson.** This thread switched topic 26 times across 36 comments and redefined its own
labels seven times; the successor posts one experiment per comment under a fixed answer contract,
with a pre-registered hypothesis, a done-when and a kill criterion for each.

Superseded and re-run under the new contract: the C4/A3 selection (made on raw reward), the
TIS comparison (a package, not a correction), the sparse codecs (implementations, not the idea),
and the pooled drift metric (engine mismatch and staleness were one number).

Seed-43 confirmation (C2/A1 vs C4/A3) completes as the last result posted here.

issues.author: RicardoDominguez
issues.body: Our aim is to predict the SWE-bench pass@1 of the final Snowball 9.97T base model after distilling on 2B tokens of SWE-smith trajectories generated by Qwen3.6-35B-A3B. We take the Snowball 3k, 9k, 18k, and 39k [intermediate checkpoints](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/snowball-intermediate) and [Grug](https://huggingface.co/penfever/grug-67b-a2b-sft-s1-wildchat-step257), and SFT them on [2B tokens](https://huggingface.co/datasets/nanoswe/swesmith-qwen3.6-35b-a3b) generated by a lightly fine-tuned variant of [Qwen3.6-35B-A3B](https://huggingface.co/nanoswe/qwen-3.6-35b-a3b-teacher) against the [SWE-smith](https://huggingface.co/datasets/SWE-bench/SWE-smith) problem set. We SFT the Snowball checkpoints at 0.21B and 0.64B token budgets, and Grug additionally at 0.37B, 1.1B, and 1.9B budgets. We evaluate the bpb of all fine-tunes on 1.3k SWE-smith trajectories generated by the teacher model. We also evaluate the pass@1 of the Grug fine-tunes. We fit two scaling laws, one relating pre-training steps and SFT budget to bpb, and a second relating bpb to pass@1. We obtain a final prediction of 33% pass@1 for the 9.97T Snowball checkpoint fine-tuned on our SFT dataset. ## Predicting bpb on teacher trajectories We use a multiplicative law. In ongoing work using pre-training checkpoints trained under constant LR (SmolLM3), we found the following law to work well: ```math \text{bpb} = E \left(1 + A\, D_{\text{pre}}^{-\alpha}\right) \left(1 + B\, D_{\text{sft}}^{-\beta}\right) ``` To account for the LR schedule of Snowball, we use the approach of [Scaling Law with Learning Rate Annealing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.11029) to model both the Grug anneal and the Snowball anneal. We thus turn $`1 + A\, D_{\text{pre}}^{-\alpha}`$ into ```math 1 + A\, S_1^{-\alpha} - C\, S_2 ``` where $`S_1 = 10^{-4} \sum_i \eta_i / \eta_{\text{peak}}`$ is the LR area over pre-training optimizer steps (proportional to $`D_{\text{pre}}`$ at constant LR, warmup counted at peak), and $`S_2 = 10^{-3} \sum_i m_i`$ is the annealing area, with momentum $`m_i = \lambda\, m_{i-1} + (\eta_{i-1} - \eta_i) / \eta_{\text{peak}}`$, $`\lambda = 0.999`$ (as in Tissue et al.), and $`\eta_{\text{peak}} = 5.28 \times 10^{-3}`$. The full law is ```math \text{bpb} = E \left(1 + A\, S_1^{-\alpha} - C\, S_2\right) \left(1 + B\, D_{\text{sft}}^{-\beta}\right) ``` with $`D_{\text{sft}}`$ in billions of tokens. We fit the six coefficients on our 13 datapoints using least squares, obtaining $`E = 0.0538,\ A = 0.278,\ \alpha = 0.783,\ C = 0.124,\ B = 0.260,\ \beta = 0.306`$, and a df-adjusted RMSE of 0.000441 bpb. Extrapolating to 9.97T pre-training tokens at 1.93B SFT tokens, we predict 0.0635 bpb. It is unclear whether calibrating the law on the much shorter Grug cooldown will extrapolate to the cooldown of Snowball. ## From bpb to pass@1 We fit the following law: ```math \log \text{pass@1} = a - b \cdot \text{bpb} ``` We fit the law using OLS on the five Grug SFTs, obtaining $`a = 5.98`$ and $`b = 39.1`$ (i.e., $`\text{pass@1} = 397\, e^{-39.1 \cdot \text{bpb}}`$), and extrapolate to the bpb predicted by the previous law, resulting in a predicted pass@1 of 33%. The 95% CI on the mean at the forecast is large: 29.3% to 37.5% pass@1. Our hunch is that the 33% prediction might be slightly conservative: fitting the law on only the three largest SFT budgets instead predicts 35%. ## Conclusion Our laws predict that fine-tuning the final Snowball checkpoint on our 2B Qwen3.6-35B-A3B dataset will result in a SWE-bench pass@1 of **33%**. If anything we expect to err low, and would not be surprised by 35%.

issues.author: mrinal-bespoke
issues.body:
Vista has a second evaluation pipeline alongside `flawed_summ` for newly published checkpoints that lack leaderboard coverage. It polls the leaderboard registry read-only, canonicalizes Hugging Face repository aliases and immutable revisions, and feeds missing agentic and non-agentic work into a durable FCFS queue.

The implementation has been exercised with a hard limit of 20 runnable production jobs: up to 8 controller-owned `flawed_summ` jobs and up to 12 missing-eval jobs. The missing-eval pool targets 8 agentic and 4 non-agentic jobs, allows either class to borrow idle capacity, and stops new admissions after repeated failures. Existing jobs are not cancelled. `JobHeldUser` entries do not count as runnable.

This is a concrete Vista implementation of #7628 and part of #6503. It currently lives in an OpenThoughts-Agent operator branch and has no public PR. The integration boundary with Marin's launcher and evaldash needs review so that checkpoint eligibility and result records retain one canonical owner.

Done when:

- The controller implementation and operational runbook are available in a public PR linked from this issue.
- The eligible-checkpoint rule, agentic and non-agentic benchmark sets, immutable model identity, retry policy, and result-publication path are reviewable.
- A canary moves one newly published checkpoint from missing coverage through one submission per missing leg to validated terminal records and leaderboard visibility without a manual queue edit.
- Repeated registry polls, controller restarts, and live `Pending`, `Started`, or numeric `Finished` rows do not create duplicate jobs.
- Behavior tests and Vista evidence cover the 20/8/12 caps, borrowable 8/4 split, failure circuit, and no-cancellation rule.
- Marin's canonical owner for checkpoint eligibility and result records is documented. Any OpenThoughts registry dependency is an explicit adapter, not a competing record store.

issues.author: mcwitt
issues.body:
On the ragged all-to-all EP backend at d6144, the first train step after a periodic eval fails with `NCCL operation ncclGroupEnd() failed: invalid argument` on most of the 64 ranks, deterministically, and the gang shuts down. The d768 rung completes 20 evals on the same code. The live hero would hit this at its first eval after the backend swap and then crash-loop through the ladder's retries, since each retry resumes from the last temporary checkpoint and reaches the same eval step.

The capacity-limited evaluator (`GrugEvalConfig.eval_current`) runs the training MoE path, so it is a second ragged all-to-all executable on the training clique with a 16x smaller all-to-all footprint. XLA registers one NCCL symmetric-memory window per executable starting at the base of the collective-memory arena and sized to that executable's footprint (`AcquireSymmetricMemory` in `xla/backends/gpu/runtime/collective_memory.cc` → `ncclCommWindowRegister` in `nccl_symmetric_memory.cc`), caches it per executable keyed by clique and device address, and keeps it until the executable or the clique is destroyed. An `NCCL_DEBUG=INFO NCCL_DEBUG_SUBSYS=REG,INIT` trace on one rank shows the two train-step executables each registering a window of 20,293,761,024 bytes at `0xbf80000000` (identical ranges, accepted), the eval registering 518,436,864 bytes at the same base (accepted), and the next train step failing at launch after a cache hit on its own window. Executables with equal footprints coexist, which is why the train step's with-hooks and without-hooks variants never collide. The dropless evaluator (`sonic_cute`) has no all-to-all and does not trigger it.

Reproduce: one rack, `launch_diagnostics.py --dp-racks 1 --moe-implementation ragged_all_to_all --master-params device --restore-from <hero step-48000> --num-steps 48004 --eval-every 2` on main `c13d1ddf27`. Runs `ra2a-rt-c13d1-48k`, `ra2a-evalnccl-c13d1`, and `ra2a-evalinfo-c13d1` (the trace) fail; `ra2a-evaldl-c13d1` with `eval_current=False` passes two evals and six steps, with dropless numbers matching the hero's step-47999 eval.

#8859 disables the capacity-limited evaluator on the ragged rungs and keeps the dropless one. Done when the capacity-limited evaluator can run between ragged train steps again, which needs XLA to register the collective-memory arena once per communicator and address executables by offset, or to key windows by allocation and deregister them on release. The Grafana hero-health `eval_regressed` signal and the Paloma chart read `eval/paloma/macro_loss` and need to move to `eval_dropless/paloma/macro_loss` while the capacity-limited series is off.

comments.author: mcwitt
comments.body: 🤖 Linking #8870: the same two-executables-one-arena design fails the other way at hero scale. With equal footprints (the plain train step and the watch-step variant) there is no `ncclGroupEnd` error; instead the first plain step after a watch step hangs on one rack, nondeterministically (steps 54071 and 54001 on two attempts, different racks, same nodes). #8859 removed the eval executable, so it avoids this issue's crash but not #8870's hang.

comments.author: mcwitt
comments.body:
🤖 Root cause found, and it is upstream of the symmetric-memory design question this issue opens with. The two aliasing windows come from one scalar: the step counter's sharding.

`_init_state` is `@jax.jit` with no explicit `out_shardings` (`experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/train.py:1006`), so `step=jnp.array(0, dtype=jnp.int32)` (`:763`) comes back under a `GSPMDSharding({replicated})`. `train_step` runs under the explicit mesh and returns `step=state.step + one` (`:933`) under a `NamedSharding`. JAX keys its compilation cache on input shardings, so the second step misses the cache and compiles a second executable, which then serves the rest of the run while the first stays alive in the cache. Every other state leaf already carries an explicit sharding and matches across the step.

`CollectiveMemoryCache` is a member of `GpuExecutable`, so two executables means two `ncclCommWindowRegister` calls over the same collective-memory arena, at the same base address, with identical size. NCCL 2.30.7 accepts the duplicate: commit `52f6d00` deleted the backing-allocation dedup loop from `symMemoryObtain`, which is present at `src/dev_runtime.cc:615` in `v2.30.4-1` and gone in `v2.30.7-1`. Nothing in the registration path checks for overlap.

The failure then comes from the lookup. `ncclDevrFindWindow` (`src/dev_runtime.cc:1401`) resolves an address to the **last** window registered there, so the eval's 518,436,864-byte window shadows the two 20,293,761,024-byte train windows at `0xbf80000000`. An access at an offset past the smaller window's size fails `ncclDevrGetLsaRankPtr`'s `offset >= winHost->size` test, which returns a bare `ncclInvalidArgument` with no WARN. That is why `NCCL_DEBUG=WARN` produces nothing and XLA itself reports `Last NCCL warning(error) log entry ''`.

Measured on one rack at d6144 (48 layers, EP64, `--watch-mode inline`, no evaluator): 128 `jit(train_step)` XLA compilations and 128 registrations of `ptr=0xbf80000000; size=20293761024` across 64 ranks, two of each per rank. The same run at 12 layers gives 64 and 64. A per-leaf `Format` diff across one step names exactly one drifting leaf: `.step`, `GSPMDSharding({replicated}, memory_kind=device)` before and `NamedSharding(mesh=Mesh('replica_dcn':1,'data':1,'expert':64,'model':1), ...)` after. It is not a tracing retrace — `JAX_EXPLAIN_CACHE_MISSES=1` reports only "never seen function" for inner functions and never for `train_step`.

Two avenues are closed. NCCL 2.31.2 does not fix this: `ra2a-8870-nccl2312-r2` ran `NCCL version 2.31.2+cuda13.3`, completed a train step and both evals, then failed character-identically to its 2.30.7 sibling `ra2a-evalnccl-c13d1` at the eval-to-train handoff on 42 of 64 ranks. NCCL's fix (`8b6b8b6`/`5a4b7fa`) is on `origin/dev` and `origin/staging` and in no tag. Upstream XLA has no fix either: `collective_memory*.{cc,h}` and `nccl_symmetric_memory.*` are byte-identical between the pinned base `dcf304bc5d` and `upstream/main`.

#8859 removed the third executable, not the aliasing. Two windows per rank are registered in every d6144 ragged run, including both that hung in #8870.

Fix: place the step counter on the sharding the train step returns it with, once the state is finalised. One executable, one window, and this collision becomes impossible rather than avoided by keeping the capacity-limited evaluator off. Note `jax.device_put` is not usable here — it asserts inside `_different_device_order_reshard` when the source is a `GSPMDSharding` whose device order differs from the mesh's — so the reshard goes through a small `jit` with `out_shardings`. The change is committed on `mcwitt/8870-repro`; verification at the hero shape is running and should show 64 compilations and 64 registrations.

One caveat for whoever reviews this: the depth dependence is unexplained. The same sharding mismatch should exist at 12 layers, yet a 12-layer run registers one window. The fix does not depend on resolving that, but the small-scale case should not be assumed to be understood.

comments.author: mcwitt
comments.body:
🤖 Fix verified at the hero shape on one rack. The run completed with 64 `jit(train_step)` XLA compilations and 64 registrations of `ptr=0xbf80000000; size=20293761024` across 64 ranks, one of each per rank, against 128 and 128 before the change. The per-leaf `Format` diff across a step now reports `identical across the step`, so the drift is gone rather than only its effect.

Configuration was d6144, 48 layers, EP64 on one NVL72 rack, `--moe-implementation ragged_all_to_all --master-params device --watch-mode inline --watch-interval 10`, no evaluator, counted with `TF_CPP_MIN_LOG_LEVEL=0 TF_CPP_VMODULE=nccl_symmetric_memory=3` and `JAX_LOG_COMPILES=1`.

One implementation note for review: `jax.device_put` cannot be used to place the counter, because it hits an assertion inside JAX's `_different_device_order_reshard` when the source is a `GSPMDSharding` whose device order differs from the mesh's. The reshard goes through a small `jit` with `out_shardings` instead, which costs nothing for a scalar.

With one executable there is one symmetric window per rank, so a second executable of any footprint can no longer shadow it, and the capacity-limited evaluator can be re-enabled once this lands. That is the condition this issue asks for, reached from the JAX side rather than by changing how XLA registers the arena.

comments.author: mcwitt
comments.body:
🤖 The aliasing is now confirmed directly at the hero's own scale, which the earlier one-rack measurements could only imply. An eleven-rack run on 2026-09-03 at the hero shape, restored from `step-54000` with the step-counter fix deliberately switched off, registered **1408 arena windows across 704 ranks — exactly two per rank** — of size 20,293,761,024 at the same base, alongside 1408 `jit_train_step` compilations and 16,896 of the 2 MiB per-thunk barrier-signal windows. That is the two-executables-one-arena condition this issue describes, observed at 704 ranks rather than 64.

The fix holds the other way at the same scale: with the step counter placed on the mesh the train step returns it with, the count is one executable and one arena window per rank.

Also worth recording here, because it bears on the symmetric-memory design question this issue opens with: the pinned PJRT wheel compiles its device kernels against `HERMETIC_NCCL_VERSION="2.29.7"` (`tensorflow.bazelrc:192`) while the runtime resolves to 2.30.7. NCCL's `ncclDevCommCompat_v22907` shim forces `ginType = NONE` and gates `deviceApiSupport` on the clique being a single LSA team. The relevant consequence for this issue is that the deployed kernel is built without 2.30's system-scope release fence in the barrier's `arrive`, and that `52f6d00` — which removed the backing-registration dedup from `symMemoryObtain` and is what lets two identical registrations over one allocation both succeed — shipped *in* 2.30.7, i.e. in the runtime we use but not in the headers we compile against. The upstream restoration (`8b6b8b6`/`5a4b7fa`, on `origin/dev`, in no tag) makes that reuse decision collective specifically because the local-cache version permits a rank-divergent register sequence that hangs.

comments.author: mcwitt
comments.body:
🤖 Fix opened as #8911: the step counter is placed on `NamedSharding(mesh, P())` once the state is final, so `train_step` compiles once and registers one symmetric window per rank. The PR carries only the placement and a CPU regression test; the diagnostics from `mcwitt/8870-repro` stay on that branch.

The capacity-limited evaluator remains off on the ragged rungs. Running it between ragged train steps under the fix has not been tested, so this issue's closing condition rests on the one-executable measurement rather than on an eval-interleaved run.

issues.author: dlwh
issues.body:
Four-stage explicit-MPMD JaxPP training can deadlock before the first loss when `jax.lax.ragged_all_to_all` uses the JAX 0.11 device-initiated NCCL path. The same nightly stack completes an exact-ring pipeline control, and the device ragged collective is bitwise exact and `7.4349x` faster in a direct EP8 benchmark. This blocks using the public device collective for the L24 pipeline target tracked in #7024.

Reproduce:
1. Check out [`0cabe5f74b`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/commit/0cabe5f74b4dae2dd438d5c8122d7d42dc3dcfec).
2. Run the [four-H100 lower-bound command](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/0cabe5f74b4dae2dd438d5c8122d7d42dc3dcfec/experiments/grug/moe/repro_jaxpp_jax011_ragged_all_to_all.README.md#h100-command). Direct ragged-all-to-all, JaxPP transfer, and their minimum two-rank composition all return exactly with checksum `202`.
3. Launch `experiments/grug/moe/run_cw_jaxpp_may_d2560.sh` on four H100x8 ranks with JAX/JAXLIB/CUDA13 plugin/PJRT `0.11.1.dev20260725`, NCCL `2.30.7`, JaxPP `7091a9b5ce02cd1a6bdc905f6a36e89370a5fba9`, L8/d2560/e64/top-k4/seq4096/b512/m16, four two-layer stages, `ragged_all_to_all`, reference attention, XLA expert GEMM, and XLA autotuning/GEMM rewrites disabled.
4. Use either GPipe or standard 1F1B with `transfer_priority`. The known runs are `/dlwh/iris-run-job-20260726-111423` and `/dlwh/iris-run-job-20260726-113121`.

GPipe stops with rank 0 in `enqueue_nccl_transfer_group -> ncclGroupEnd`, ranks 1-2 in `recv_done_impl`, and rank 3 in `backend_compile_and_load`. Transfer-priority 1F1B stops with ranks 0-1 in DIME `enqueue_nccl_transfer_group`, rank 2 compiling, and rank 3 in PJRT execution. Both hold about `56.8-57.6 GiB` per active GPU with 0% memory activity and emit no loss or MFU. The [research logbook](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/0cabe5f74b4dae2dd438d5c8122d7d42dc3dcfec/.agents/logbooks/jaxpp-grug-moe.md#2026-07-26-0450-pdt---gpipe-and-transfer-priority-retain-the-device-ragged-deadlock) records the controls and full rank evidence.

Expected: all four ranks complete finite training steps, or JaxPP reports a bounded coordination error instead of waiting indefinitely in mixed transfer, compile, and execution states.

The minimum primitive composition passes, so the smallest known failing boundary still includes the four-stage training graph. This package is ready to adapt for an upstream report, but no NVIDIA issue has been filed.

comments.author: claude[bot]
comments.body:
🤖 **Plan:**
- [x] Actionability check — issue is well-specified (pins, run IDs, isolation matrix), keep as tracking issue
- [x] Duplicate-work preflight (#7024 tracks the thread; PR #7079 is FP8, not this deadlock)
- [x] Root-cause analysis + proposed approach
- [x] Scope decision: no self-contained Marin fix → analysis comment, no PR

# Research

The hang is in the JAX `0.11.1.dev20260725` **device-initiated NCCL path**, triggered only when JaxPP's explicit inter-stage DIME transfers coexist with device `jax.lax.ragged_all_to_all` in the four-stage MoE graph. It is not a Marin logic bug and not fixable in-repo. The isolation matrix in the logbook pins the boundary:

- Direct device `ragged_all_to_all` on two H100s: **exact**, checksum `202`, `7.4349x` faster than the host path.
- JaxPP transfer-only control and the two-rank transfer+ragged composition: **pass**.
- Matched nightly **exact-ring** pipeline (no explicit ragged transfer): **4/4**, finite loss `8.797631`.
- Four-stage device-ragged + JaxPP transfer: **deadlocks** under GPipe, standard 1F1B, and transfer-priority alike — ranks split across `enqueue_nccl_transfer_group → ncclGroupEnd`, `recv_done_impl`, `backend_compile_and_load`, and PJRT execution; ~57 GiB held per GPU at 0% memory activity, no loss/MFU.

So the smallest known failing boundary is the full four-stage training graph; every reduced schedule and the primitive composition pass. The device NCCL communicator setup also required pinning `nvidia-nccl-cu13==2.30.7` to clear a `ncclDevCommCreate` segfault, and autotuning/GEMM rewrites had to be disabled to reach the transfer stage — after which execution deadlocks.

**Relevant code** (branch `research/jaxpp-grug-moe` @ `0cabe5f74b`, tracks #7024):
- [`ep_ragged_all_to_all.py#L77`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/0cabe5f74b4dae2dd438d5c8122d7d42dc3dcfec/lib/levanter/src/levanter/grug/_moe/ep_ragged_all_to_all.py#L77) / [`#L105`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/0cabe5f74b4dae2dd438d5c8122d7d42dc3dcfec/lib/levanter/src/levanter/grug/_moe/ep_ragged_all_to_all.py#L105) — dispatch/combine device collective
- [`repro_jaxpp_jax011_ragged_all_to_all.README.md`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/0cabe5f74b4dae2dd438d5c8122d7d42dc3dcfec/experiments/grug/moe/repro_jaxpp_jax011_ragged_all_to_all.README.md) — two-rank primitive boundary (passes)
- [`jaxpp_jax_0_11_inline.patch`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/0cabe5f74b4dae2dd438d5c8122d7d42dc3dcfec/experiments/grug/moe/jaxpp_jax_0_11_inline.patch) — JaxPP↔JAX 0.11 compat shim
- [logbook 04:50 PDT](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/0cabe5f74b4dae2dd438d5c8122d7d42dc3dcfec/.agents/logbooks/jaxpp-grug-moe.md#2026-07-26-0450-pdt---gpipe-and-transfer-priority-retain-the-device-ragged-deadlock) — full rank evidence

# Proposed approach

No Marin code change resolves this — the deadlock is in the JAX/NCCL/JaxPP device-collective stack. Recommend two independent tracks for a human to sign off on:

1. **File upstream.** The two-rank reproducer already isolates the transfer+ragged composition and passes, while the four-stage graph hangs; that is the evidence an upstream bug needs. File against JaxPP (NVIDIA) and/or JAX with the pinned environment and the mixed-state rank dump, and link it back here. The issue notes the package is "ready to adapt for an upstream report" but none is filed yet.
2. **Unblock #7024 in the interim.** The nightly **exact-ring** pipeline completes 4/4 with finite loss, so the L24 target is not gated on the device collective. Fall back to the exact-ring transfer path (accepting the ~7.4x transport loss on `ragged_all_to_all`) until upstream fixes the device path, rather than blocking pipeline-parallel MoE training on it.

I am not opening a PR: the fix is upstream and the in-repo decision (upstream report vs. exact-ring fallback for #7024) needs a human owner.

comments.author: dlwh
comments.body:
🤖 Boundary update: the earlier conclusion that this was already isolated below Marin/JaxPP was too strong.

Two additional four-rank H100 gates now pass exactly:
- One microbatch: four two-H100 MPMD ranks, three forward plus three reverse DIME transfers, and an exact device ragged collective in every stage task; checksum `202`.
- Sixteen microbatches: 96 logical transfers and 128 stage tasks with repeated receive-buffer reuse; checksum `3,232`.

Both jobs returned every rank from init, lower, eval, barrier, and shutdown with no watchdog, signal, or retry. Evidence snapshot: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/commit/19c18ac4151ddcb650c4ea54c12b96f3df26e018.

That rules out rank count, bidirectional topology, repeated tiny transfers, and receive-buffer reuse at tiny payload as sufficient causes. The remaining boundary is the full L8 training graph or payload/compute compilation interleaved with multiple communicators.

issues.title: [grug] JaxPP device-ragged pipelines deadlock during DIME transfer

issues.author: dlwh
issues.body:
<!-- experiment-tldr:start -->

Automatic JaxPP DualPipeV is now the validated Grug MoE pipeline implementation. The canonical example in #8739 supports automatic ZeroBubble and DualPipeV schedules through one state, autodiff, and MPMD orchestration path. Parameters and Adam state are initialized on their owning stages, so the implementation does not materialize the full 67B training state. The root `pipeline` extra installs the pinned JaxPP and CUDA dependencies through the ordinary workspace sync. It requires NCCL 2.31.2; NCCL 2.30.7 hangs the grouped-transfer path on current JaxPP, while the final two-node H100x8 gate completed with 2.31.2.

The final Snowball 67B-A2B result uses 64 H100s, PP8 x EP8, 16 logical DualPipeV stages, sequence length 8192, batch 256, 32 microbatches, BF16 parameters and compute, and full rematerialization. Median step time is `3.475980327s`, throughput is `603,326.77` tokens/s, median analytic MFU is `19.45529%`, and peak memory is `59,153,094,656` bytes/device. The matched batch-128, 16-microbatch control reaches `543,490.02` tokens/s and `17.52575%` median analytic MFU. Doubling the microbatch count improves median throughput and MFU by `11.01%` with no measured memory increase. Final synthetic-data loss differs by `4.02e-5` between the two runs.

The no-JaxPP baseline uses ordinary Grug training with FSDP8 x EP8 on the same 64 H100s. Batch 256 OOMs before step 0 with a `101.02 GiB` allocation request per device. Batch 64 succeeds at `1.931756s` median step time, `271,404.87` tokens/s, `8.75191%` median analytic MFU, and `29,017,027,044` bytes/device peak. DualPipeV provides `2.223x` the median token throughput and MFU while using `2.039x` the memory. The global batches differ by `4x`, so this comparison measures the viable configurations rather than isolating schedule efficiency at a matched batch.

This meets the practical target for the current work. The measured DualPipeV point is `0.545` percentage point below 20% analytic MFU, and further microbatch scaling is unlikely to justify another 64-H100 experiment without a production workload. The profile attributes the remaining gap primarily to pipeline dependency and SendRecv waiting, especially at the endpoint pair. Attention kernels account for roughly `2.05-4.73%` of exclusive GPU time per physical rank; FSDP and MoE all-gather/reduce-scatter costs are secondary.

Command buffers remain disabled in the validated recipe. JAX 0.11.0 has an XLA mixed-clique initialization bug, while the tested nightly exposes JaxPP DiME multi-communicator initialization and execution deadlocks on the full DualPipeV topology. Deterministic communicator preinitialization fixes the reduced gate but not the full Snowball run. Track that work separately in #7655; it does not block the no-command-buffer result.

PR #8739 is open and awaits review. The issue should remain open until that PR lands.

<!-- experiment-tldr:end -->

Current baseline

| Area | Current state |
| --- | --- |
| Implementation | Automatic JaxPP DualPipeV in #8739 |
| Model | Snowball 67B-A2B: 67.08B total / about 2.01B active, 26 layers, d2560, 256 experts, top-k 4, sequence 8192 |
| Topology | 64 H100s; PP8 x EP8; 16 logical stages mapped to 8 physical ranks |
| Precision | BF16 parameters, compute, and output; full rematerialization |
| Batch | Global batch 256; 32 microbatches |
| Performance | `3.475980327s` median step; `603,326.77` tokens/s; `19.45529%` median analytic MFU |
| Memory | `59,153,094,656` bytes/device peak |
| No-JaxPP comparison | FSDP8 x EP8 at batch 64: `1.931756s`, `271,404.87` tokens/s, `8.75191%` median analytic MFU, `29,017,027,044` bytes/device peak |
| Runtime caveat | XLA command buffers disabled; follow-up tracked in #7655 |

Decision log

- Use the model-specific Grug implementation as a canonical example that can be adapted to another model. Keep generic mechanics in `levanter.pipeline`; do not hide model partitioning behind a generic high-level pipeline module.
- Keep the benchmark automatic-only. Sequential staged-loss and gradient parity remain the independent numerical check without a second MPMD execution path.
- Use automatic DualPipeV for the validated Snowball recipe. Sixteen logical stages map two stages to each of eight physical pipeline ranks and reduce the warmup/cooldown bubble relative to the eight-stage automatic ZeroBubble schedule.
- Initialize parameters and optimizer state stage-locally. Full-state initialization exceeded H100 memory before pipeline execution.
- Keep the validated 16-stage layer placement. Profiled physical-rank compute differs by up to `1.414x`, but moving one indivisible layer only moves the heavy rank and cannot remove the endpoint bubble.
- Use 32 microbatches for the best measured throughput point. Compared with the matched 16-microbatch control, it improves median throughput and MFU by `11.01%` at identical peak memory.
- Keep command buffers disabled until #7655 has a full-topology fix. Increasing rendezvous timeouts and communicator preinitialization alone did not make the full run execute.
- Treat `19.45529%` as an analytic MFU estimate. The existing FLOP model uses full attention and therefore slightly overestimates work for sliding-window layers.

Prior baseline and negative results

- The earlier explicit-MPMD L24/d2560/e64/top-k4/sequence-4096 result remains a useful historical baseline: `18.2583%` mean MFU and `414,059.10` tokens/s at batch 8192 with 256 microbatches. It is a different model shape and should not be compared directly with the Snowball result.
- Ordinary FSDP8 x EP8 at batch 256 OOMs before step 0 after XLA rematerializes an inefficient batch-to-FSDP reshard and requests `101.02 GiB` per device. Batch 64 fits and reaches `271,404.87` tokens/s and `8.75191%` median analytic MFU with `29.017 GB` peak memory. Its final synthetic-data loss is `0.671852`, within `4.92e-4` of the DualPipeV result.
- Four-stage automatic ZeroBubble works, but eight physical stages with 16 microbatches reached only about `12.83%` mean MFU on the matched Snowball comparison. Long-run DualPipeV reached `16.96%` mean and `17.52%` median MFU at 16 microbatches, a roughly `32%` mean throughput improvement.
- A profile-guided endpoint layer rebalance improved the eight-stage automatic ZeroBubble schedule by only about `1.4%`. The remaining wait is schedule-level.
- Snowball sequence length 32K exceeded memory at PP8. A PP13 experiment was abandoned in favor of validating sequence length 8K.
- Automatic ZeroBubble and explicit 1F1B with command buffers enabled failed during executable initialization on the production JAX pin. The tested JAX nightly passes the reduced XLA initialization gate but deadlocks in JaxPP DiME communicator setup or subsequent execution at full scale.
- Deterministic DiME communicator preinitialization succeeds on a reduced PP8 x EP8 DualPipeV gate. The full Snowball topology still hangs before step 0 with ranks split across runtime compilation, NCCL group completion, and receive waits.
- Attention, Hopper MoE kernels, and intra-stage all-gather/reduce-scatter are not the first optimization target in the representative profile. SendRecv duration is primarily a waiting proxy, not wire-transfer time.

Helpful links

- Implementation PR: #8739
- Command-buffer and DiME follow-up: #7655
- Earlier explicit-MPMD snapshot: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/commit/ecb724da6e
- Earlier explicit baseline: https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/jaxpp-rno2a-ring-l24-e64k4-b8192-s4096-p4m256-20260711-0107
- Earlier research logbook: `.agents/logbooks/jaxpp-grug-moe-2.md`

Next steps

1. Land #8739 and use its documented Snowball command as the reproducible pipeline baseline.
2. Keep command-buffer investigation in #7655. Do not block the no-command-buffer training path on it.
3. Revisit pipeline optimization only for a concrete production workload. The next target is endpoint dependency scheduling, not attention or MoE kernel replacement.

Conclusion

The pipeline-parallel Grug MoE path is complete for the current goal. Automatic DualPipeV trains the Snowball 67B-A2B architecture on 64 H100s at `19.45529%` median analytic MFU and `603,326.77` tokens/s with stage-local model and optimizer state. Ordinary FSDP8 x EP8 fits at batch 64 and reaches `8.75191%` median analytic MFU; its batch-256 configuration OOMs. The implementation is ready in #8739. Command buffers are the remaining optional performance and runtime follow-up.

---

🤖 **Not opening a PR — this is a hardware-dependent experiment tracking issue, not an agent-actionable code task.**

# Research

The definition of done here is a *measured MFU number* from a real training run on `cw-us-east-02a` (4× gd-8xh100ib). That requires GPU cluster access, `jaxpp` runtime dependency handling, a 4-node H100 launch harness, and a schedule sweep — a multi-phase research effort, not a self-contained fix. An agent PR can't close it.

Two state discrepancies worth flagging, since they'll trip up whoever picks this up:

- The JaxPP branch described in the body isn't reachable from `main`. `GrugTrainerConfig` ([`train.py#L53-L71`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/experiments/grug/moe/train.py#L53-L71)) has **no `pipeline` field**, and `grep -ri jaxpp` over the repo returns nothing. The `pipeline` mesh axis / `jaxpp.treduce` / stage-boundary work referenced in the issue lives on an unpushed branch.
- The logbook link `.agents/logbooks/jaxpp-grug-moe.md` doesn't exist (no `.agents/logbooks/` dir on `main`).

**Related but distinct prior work:** `origin/weaver/investigate-pipeline-parallelism` already explores PP for Grug MoE, but via a **delayed-gradient / staleness simulation** path, not JaxPP on hardware — `experiments/grug/moe_delay/` (`delay_optim.py`, `pp_throughput_model.py`, `launch.py`) plus `docs/reports/pipeline-parallel-moe-staleness.md`. Its throughput model and iso-loss token-tax analysis are directly relevant priors for interpreting a real JaxPP MFU number, but it's a different implementation and doesn't satisfy this issue's goal.

# Proposed next steps (for a human with cluster access)

1. Push the JaxPP branch (the `GrugTrainerConfig.pipeline` path) so it's reviewable, and add the logbook the body references.
2. Land `jaxpp` runtime dependency handling (optional-dep guard behind the pipeline path).
3. Add the 4-node H100 launch harness for `cw-us-east-02a`.
4. Run the schedule sweep on the May d=2560 shape (seq 4096, 256 experts, top-k 4, expert axis 8, replica 1; reduce experts if needed for a debug run) and extract MFU from tracker/log output.

Happy to take on any *code-only, testable* slice of this — e.g. the optional-dep guard, the mesh-reshape-into-microbatches logic, or MFU extraction — if it's split out with concrete acceptance criteria that don't require a live GPU run. Point me at the branch and I'll pick one up.

## Summary

This issue tracks JaxPP pipeline parallelism for Grug MoE training on 4x 8xH100 CoreWeave. The explicit `jaxpp.experimental.mpmd` implementation partitions model weights and optimizer state by stage and runs the requested 24-layer, d2560, sequence-4096 model with GPipe, `std_1f1b`, and queue-correct interleaved GPipe schedules.

The current performance shape uses 64 experts with top-k 4. The best measured point is explicit `std_1f1b`, batch8192/m256, four six-layer stages, ring expert parallelism, CuTe FA4, and eight-warp Pallas-Triton grouped GEMM on RNO2A: mean MFU `18.2583`, p50 `18.3654`, p90 `18.3830`, and `414,059.10` tokens/s. Scaling from m128 to m256 added only `0.1248` mean MFU points, so pipeline occupancy is saturated `1.7417` points below the 20-MFU target.

Profile-guided routing work removed three large rank-2 floating scatter families with explicit Triton kernels and custom VJPs. H100 value/VJP parity and optimized-HLO checks pass, but a pinned 10-step reduced A/B was neutral: bulk ring averaged `9.1735` central MFU versus `9.1595` for `ring_fused`. The backend is not being scaled to L24.

An EP-local QuACK/Sonic grouped-MLP adapter is the first direct expert-kernel result to clear the performance gate: at the exact e64/top-k4/d2560 EP8 microbatch, median forward improves `1.160x` and forward-backward improves `1.108x`. Its approximate fused SwiGLU is now exposed only through explicit research backend `ring_quack_approx`. A paired 10-step one-node training gate stays finite with final relative loss delta `+0.01356%`, while mean MFU improves `4.00%` and median duration falls `4.04%`. The reduced JaxPP gate is next; the 4% whole-step gain alone does not project the current L24 best above 20 MFU.

comments.author: dlwh
comments.body:
🤖 Update: r11f isolates an XLA MPMD autotuning deadlock

- All 32 ranks completed JAX and NCCL_EP bootstrap. Stage 0 entered first-forward compilation while stages 1-3 entered JaxPP DIME rendezvous. Native stacks on every stage-0 process converged on `xla::Autotuner::Autotune -> DistributedKeyValueStore::Get`; downstream ranks waited independently for DIME keys. CPU activity was effectively idle.
- OpenXLA defaults `xla_gpu_shard_autotuning=true`. Its config assigner fingerprints the complete HLO module, assigns candidates across every compiler process, and waits for one result key from every process. JaxPP MPMD stages compile different modules, so the expected keys cannot match. r11f was deadlocked, not merely compiling slowly.

- Run: `/dlwh/ep-ring-data4-ep2-fused-fp32acc-r20-20260727` on one RNO2A H100x8, exact d2560/i1280/e64/top-k4/m32/seq4096 geometry, 10 warmups, 50 samples, 0.70 XLA fraction, and no retries.
- Gate: loss/output/every gradient leaf relative-L2 `<=0.002`, exact drops, no data-axis collective inside local VAG, and composed MFU above `20.0`. A passing direct result must still clear a reduced JaxPP gate before L24.

issues.author: dlwh
issues.body:
## Summary

When a TPU worker restarts into a bad environment, Levanter can raise a mesh-shape `ValueError` before it raises the more helpful `No accelerator found` error.

## What happened

In the Grug MoE Ray runs on March 8, 2026, we saw restart fallout where one retried worker logged:

- `A Google TPU may be present on this machine, but either a TPU-enabled jaxlib or libtpu is not installed. Falling back to cpu.`
- then later failed with:
  - `ValueError: ICI product 4 does not divide devices_per_slice 1.`

The confusing part is that `TrainerConfig.initialize()` appears to intend to fail fast on missing accelerators on non-Darwin platforms, but that check happens after mesh validation.

## Suspected cause

In `lib/levanter/src/levanter/trainer.py`:

- `initialize()` calls `self._validate_and_set_defaults()` before the `require_accelerator` / `jax.default_backend() == "cpu"` guard.
- `_validate_and_set_defaults()` immediately touches `self.mesh_axis_specs`.
- `mesh_axis_specs` calls `self.mesh.axis_shapes(jax.device_count(), self.num_slices)`.

So on a bad restart path, CPU fallback can produce a mesh-shape failure first, and the intended accelerator check never runs.

## Why this matters

This makes restart/debug flows noisier and obscures root cause. Instead of getting a direct accelerator error, the user sees a secondary mesh-shape error.

## Suggested fix

Move the `require_accelerator` / backend check earlier in `initialize()`, before `_validate_and_set_defaults()` / mesh validation, or otherwise explicitly guard mesh validation when `jax.default_backend() == "cpu"` on accelerator-required runs.

## References

- `lib/levanter/src/levanter/trainer.py`
- observed error sequence in Grug MoE Ray run: `ray-run-grug-moe-q32a4b-v5p64-bs320-ep4-e64-k4-cf1p1-rom-r1-20260308`

comments.author: ethantsliu
comments.body:

[`TrainerConfig.initialize()`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/20d35b9019c1b00ba752406de77309c23aebf5b4/lib/levanter/src/levanter/trainer.py#L983-L1006) validates `mesh_axis_specs` before resolving `require_accelerator` and checking the JAX backend. When a TPU worker falls back to one CPU device, the configured accelerator mesh can therefore raise an ICI shape error before the missing-accelerator guard runs.

### Proposed Fix

Resolve the platform-dependent default and reject a CPU backend before `_validate_and_set_defaults()`. Cover the ordering with a startup regression that uses a CPU backend and an incompatible mesh.
